options: Remove the field descriptions from the schema to save tokens
Define the fields in a strict JSON schema and use structured outputs
Raise the temperature so the model explores more phrasings
Validate the parsed result in code and send failures to review or retry
End the prompt with 'please reply in valid JSON'
answer: Define the fields in a strict JSON schema and use structured outputs
Validate the parsed result in code and send failures to review or retry
questions.explain: Structured outputs with a strict schema enforce field names and required fields, and code validation catches wrong values. Polite requests, higher temperature and thinner schemas make failures more likely.
questions.teach: Language models can extract entities and fields into JSON, but free-form JSON drifts: fields go missing or get renamed. Structured outputs constrain generation to a JSON schema you supply, so required fields and names are enforced. Code-side validation remains the safety net for values that are well-formed but wrong.
hints: Separate two failure types: the shape of the output is wrong, or the shape is right but a value is wrong. A robust design handles both, with one mechanism for each.
Asking politely for JSON is a request, not a guarantee. Look for the option that makes the model's output conform to a declared structure.
More randomness makes field names less stable, and stripping field descriptions removes hints the model uses to fill fields correctly. Both move in the wrong direction.
questions.deep: For fixed document types (invoices, receipts), Content Understanding or Document Intelligence prebuilt models return typed fields with confidence and grounding, which is often better than prompting a chat model.

questions.prompt: A forum policy needs a finer severity scale than the four values this code prints. Which change returns all eight severity levels?
questions.code:
from azure.ai.contentsafety import ContentSafetyClient
from azure.ai.contentsafety.models import AnalyzeTextOptions
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

client = ContentSafetyClient(ENDPOINT, DefaultAzureCredential())
result = client.analyze_text(AnalyzeTextOptions(text=comment))
for item in result.categories_analysis:
    print(item.category, item.severity)
options: Read item.score instead of item.severity
Call client.analyze_image instead of analyze_text
Pass halt_on_blocklist_hit=True to AnalyzeTextOptions
Pass output_type="EightSeverityLevels" to AnalyzeTextOptions
answer: Pass output_type="EightSeverityLevels" to AnalyzeTextOptions
questions.explain: output_type="EightSeverityLevels" makes text analysis return 0 to 7 instead of 0, 2, 4, 6. Blocklist settings, image analysis and a nonexistent score field do not change the scale.
questions.teach: ContentSafetyClient.analyze_text takes an AnalyzeTextOptions request and returns categories_analysis: one entry per harm category with a severity. By default text severities come back as 0, 2, 4 or 6. AnalyzeTextOptions also accepts blocklist names for custom term lists and an output type that switches to the full eight-level scale.
hints: The change belongs in the request, because the service decides which scale to return before the response reaches your loop. Look at options that add something to the request object.
Blocklists deal with custom banned terms and whether to stop at the first match; they do not change how severity is reported for the harm categories.
Analysing images uses the trimmed scale only, and there is no score attribute that secretly holds finer values. The option you want names the output format explicitly.
questions.deep: The enum form is AnalyzeTextOutputType.EIGHT_SEVERITY_LEVELS. ContentSafetyClient accepts AzureKeyCredential or an Entra credential such as DefaultAzureCredential; with Entra you need a custom subdomain endpoint and the Cognitive Services User role.

questions.prompt: A retailer must translate 40,000 Word manuals into five languages, keep the formatting, and always render its brand terms the same way. Which option fits?
options: Azure Translator document translation with a glossary
A language model prompt per page with no terminology list
Speech translation on a narrated version of each manual
Content Understanding with the prebuilt-layout analyzer
answer: Azure Translator document translation with a glossary
questions.explain: Document translation handles whole Word files in bulk while preserving formatting, and a glossary enforces brand terms. Speech, ad hoc prompts and layout extraction miss one or more requirements.
questions.teach: Azure Translator offers text translation for strings and document translation for whole files. Document translation keeps the source structure and formatting (Word, PDF, slides) and runs asynchronously over storage containers, which suits large batches. Glossaries pin how specific terms are translated, so brand and product names stay consistent.
hints: Three requirements: very large volume of files, formatting preserved, and fixed terminology. A per-page prompt meets none of the three well, especially the last one.
Speech is about audio, and nothing here is spoken. Layout extraction reads structure out of documents but does not translate anything.
Look for a translation service mode that takes whole files rather than strings, plus a feature that fixes how named terms are translated.
questions.deep: LLM-powered translation flows are also in the outline; they shine for tone or domain adaptation, but you must supply terminology in the prompt and handle formatting yourself. Custom Translator trains domain models when glossaries are not enough.

questions.prompt: What kind of query does this code send, and how are the result lists combined?
questions.code:
vector_query = VectorizedQuery(
    vector=embed("lightweight tent for windy ridges"),
    k_nearest_neighbors=5,
    fields="contentVector",
)
results = search_client.search(
    search_text="lightweight tent windy ridge",
    vector_queries=[vector_query],
    top=5,
)
options: Pure vector; search_text is ignored when vector_queries is set
Hybrid; keyword and vector results are merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
Two separate queries whose results the client must merge
Semantic; the vector re-ranks the keyword results
answer: Hybrid; keyword and vector results are merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
questions.explain: Sending search_text and vector_queries together is a hybrid query, and the service fuses the BM25 and vector rankings with RRF. Semantic ranking needs query_type set, and nothing is merged client-side.
questions.teach: Azure AI Search supports keyword (BM25) search on searchable text fields, vector search on vector fields, and hybrid search, which runs both in one request and merges the ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Semantic ranking is a separate, optional step that re-ranks the top results with a language model and can add captions and answers.
hints: Count how many kinds of input the request carries. There is a plain text string and there is a vector query. A request carrying both kinds is the defining feature of one query type.
Both inputs go into one search call, and one result set comes back. So the service, not your code, must be combining two ranked lists into one.

Semantic re-ranking is switched on by its own parameter, which this code does not set. The merge algorithm used here works on ranks, not raw scores, so lists on different scales can be combined fairly.
questions.deep: VectorizedQuery takes a vector you computed; VectorizableTextQuery lets the service vectorize the text with the index's vectorizer. Hybrid plus semantic ranking is the combination Microsoft's own relevance tests rank highest for RAG.

questions.prompt: Semantic ranker is enabled on the service, and the index has a semantic configuration named manuals-semantic. What must you add to this call to get semantically re-ranked results?
questions.code:
results = search_client.search(
    search_text="boots that stay dry in snow",
    top=10,
)
options: vector_queries=[VectorizedQuery(...)] and nothing else
filter="semantic eq true"
query_type="semantic" and semantic_configuration_name="manuals-semantic"
query_language="en-us" and nothing else
answer: query_type="semantic" and semantic_configuration_name="manuals-semantic"
questions.explain: query_type="semantic" turns on re-ranking and semantic_configuration_name picks which configuration's fields to use. Vectors, a language hint or a filter do not invoke the semantic ranker.
questions.teach: Semantic ranking is opt-in per request. The index holds a semantic configuration that names the title, content and keyword fields the ranker should read. A query asks for it by setting the query type to semantic and naming the configuration; the service then re-ranks the top keyword or hybrid results with a language understanding model.
hints: Enabling the ranker on the service and defining a configuration in the index are both prerequisites. The query itself still has to ask for semantic ranking explicitly.
An index can hold several semantic configurations, so the request has to say which one to use. Look for the option that both switches the mode and names the configuration.
Adding a vector query makes the request hybrid, not semantic. A language hint alone changes nothing about ranking, and filters only narrow results by field values.
questions.deep: If the index defines a default semantic configuration you can omit the name, but naming it is explicit and exam-safe. Semantic ranking also returns captions and answers when you request them.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement to the index field attribute that enables it.
rows: Restrict results to category eq 'boots'
Order results by price, lowest first
Show a count of products per brand in a sidebar
Match words the user types inside the description
options: filterable
searchable
sortable
facetable
key
answer: filterable
sortable
facetable
searchable
questions.explain: Filters need filterable, ordering needs sortable, per-value counts need facetable, and full-text matching needs searchable. The key attribute only identifies documents.
questions.teach: Every field in an Azure AI Search index carries attributes that decide what queries can do with it. Searchable fields are analysed for full-text search, filterable fields support $filter expressions, sortable fields support $orderby, facetable fields return counts per value, and exactly one string field is the document key. Attributes cost storage, so enable only what you use.
hints: Read each row for the query operation it describes: excluding documents, ordering them, counting them by value, or matching words inside text.
Excluding documents by an exact value and ordering them by a value are two different operations, each with its own attribute, even though both read the same kind of field.
Counting products per brand is what powers the sidebar navigation on shopping sites. One option is unused: it identifies each document uniquely rather than enabling a query feature.
questions.deep: Changing most attributes on an existing field requires rebuilding the index, so plan them up front. In the Python SDK, SearchableField sets searchable by default while SimpleField is for filter, sort and facet use.

questions.prompt: Match each indexing or query need to the Azure AI Search feature that handles it.
rows: Make a search for 'cheval' also match the French plural 'chevaux'
Read printed text from scanned pages during indexing
Tag part numbers using your own Azure Function
Turn each chunk into a vector during indexing
options: Azure OpenAI Embedding skill
Key Phrase Extraction skill
OCR skill
A French language analyzer on the field
Shaper skill
Custom Web API skill
answer: A French language analyzer on the field
OCR skill
Custom Web API skill
Azure OpenAI Embedding skill
questions.explain: Stemming is a language analyzer's job, OCR reads scanned text, Custom Web API calls your Function, and the Azure OpenAI Embedding skill vectorizes chunks during indexing.
questions.teach: Analyzers and skills work at different stages. An analyzer processes text in searchable fields, at indexing and query time, breaking it into tokens and normalising them (for example stemming French plurals). Skills run in a skillset during indexing to enrich content: built-in skills such as OCR or Azure OpenAI Embedding, and custom skills such as Custom Web API, which calls your own endpoint.
hints: First decide for each row whether it changes how words are tokenised and matched, or whether it adds new content during indexing. The first kind is an analyzer, the second kind is a skill.
Matching singular and plural word forms in one language is a linguistic rule applied to text in a field. Reading scanned pages and generating vectors add new data to the enriched document instead.
When the logic is yours and runs in an Azure Function, the skill must call out to your endpoint over HTTP. Two options are unused: one reshapes data, one extracts key phrases.
questions.deep: Analyzers are set per field and mostly cannot change on an existing field without a rebuild. Built-in Foundry Tools skills use your attached Foundry resource for billing only, while the embedding skill calls your own deployment for processing.

questions.prompt: A team ingests mixed PDFs, slide decks exported to PDF, and scanned forms into a RAG index. They want clean Markdown with tables preserved, descriptions of charts and diagrams, and chunks ready for embedding, with no custom model training. What should they use?
options: A Document Intelligence custom extraction model trained on labelled samples
Content Safety text analysis on each page
The Text Split skill applied to the raw PDF bytes
Content Understanding with the prebuilt-documentSearch analyzer
answer: Content Understanding with the prebuilt-documentSearch analyzer
questions.explain: prebuilt-documentSearch outputs layout-aware Markdown, figure descriptions and embedding-ready chunks with no training. A custom extraction model needs labelled data, and the other options produce no usable content.
questions.teach: Document Intelligence and Content Understanding overlap on OCR and layout but aim at different jobs. Document Intelligence centres on extracting fields, tables and layout from documents, with prebuilt and custom trained models. Content Understanding uses generative models across modalities and returns grounded Markdown or schema JSON, and its prebuilt-documentSearch analyzer is built for RAG ingestion, including figure descriptions and chunking.
hints: Note the words 'no custom model training'. Any option that starts with labelling samples to train a model breaks that constraint, however accurate it might become.
Describing a chart in words requires a model that interprets images, not one that only reads characters. Splitting raw file bytes produces chunks of binary noise, not Markdown.
Safety analysis scores harm and produces no content for an index. Look for the analyzer whose stated purpose is preparing documents for retrieval-augmented generation.
questions.deep: Rule of thumb: fixed forms where you need specific fields, think Document Intelligence or a Content Understanding domain analyzer; content for an agent or RAG to reason over, think Content Understanding Markdown. Content Understanding is also a skill in Azure AI Search.

questions.prompt: After adding an Azure OpenAI Embedding skill to the skillset, only documents changed since the last run receive vectors. Which call is missing before run_indexer so every document is reprocessed?
options: indexer_client.reset_indexer("manuals-indexer")
indexer_client.create_data_source_connection(data_source)
search_client.upload_documents(documents=[])
indexer_client.get_indexer_status("manuals-indexer")
answer: indexer_client.reset_indexer("manuals-indexer")
questions.explain: reset_indexer clears the indexer's change-tracking state so run_indexer reprocesses every document with the new skill. Status reads, a new data source and an empty upload leave the high-water mark in place.
questions.teach: Indexers track a high-water mark through change detection, so a normal run only processes new or changed source documents. When you change the skillset, unchanged documents are skipped and never get the new enrichment. Resetting the indexer clears its change-tracking state so the next run processes everything again.
hints: The symptom is that unchanged documents are skipped. Ask what the indexer remembers between runs that makes it skip them, and how you would make it forget.
Reading the indexer's status tells you what happened but changes nothing. Creating another data source connection points at the same blobs and does not clear any memory.
Uploading an empty list of documents to the index does nothing to the indexer's own tracking. The answer is a call on the indexer client that clears its state.
questions.deep: On large indexes a full reset is expensive; enrichment caching with incremental enrichment can reprocess only the skills that changed. Also remember that a run can report success while individual documents fail within maxFailedItems; get_indexer_status returns the execution history with per-document errors.

questions.prompt: Match each workload to the most appropriate model category.
rows: On-device intent classification with tight memory limits
Complex, multistep policy reasoning
Question answering over an image and text prompt
Converting passages to vectors for similarity search
options: Embedding model
Multimodal model
Large reasoning-capable language model
Small language model
answer: Small language model
Large reasoning-capable language model
Multimodal model
Embedding model
questions.explain: Choose the smallest sufficient model: SLMs fit constrained devices, capable LLMs fit complex reasoning, multimodal models consume images, and embedding models produce vectors.
questions.teach: A model is chosen for the job, not for its size alone. Small language models fit tight memory and latency budgets, large reasoning-capable models handle multistep logic, multimodal models accept more than text such as images, and embedding models return vectors instead of prose so that similar passages can be found. The exam habit is to pick the smallest model that clearly does the job.
hints: Read each workload for the clue about what goes in and what must come out. One row is about the shape of the input (an image next to a text prompt), one is about the shape of the output (numbers rather than words), and two are about how hard the thinking is or how little hardware there is.

Place the two extremes first. The row with tight memory limits needs the lightweight option built for constrained devices, and the row that needs several dependent reasoning steps needs the option at the opposite end of the capability scale.

For the remaining rows, ask what a model of each category actually returns. A model whose output is a list of numbers is for similarity search, not for chatting, and the row that mixes a picture with a text question needs a model that can take both kinds of input. Each option is used once.
questions.deep: Embedding models never generate answers, and a chat model is not a substitute for one in a vector index. Check a model's supported input types in the catalogue instead of assuming it is multimodal, and remember that routing easy work to a small model and keeping a capable model for hard cases is a standard cost lever. Microsoft Learn: Foundry Models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/foundry-models/concepts/models-sold-directly-by-azure

questions.prompt: A team needs one Azure resource boundary for Foundry projects, models, agents, evaluations, and Foundry Tools such as Speech, Vision, Language, and Content Understanding. What should it create?
options: A Microsoft Foundry resource with kind AIServices
An Azure OpenAI resource that hosts only model deployments and OpenAI-compatible inference endpoints
A classic Foundry hub used as the shared resource for all new Foundry capabilities
A Foundry project created without a parent Foundry resource boundary
answer: A Microsoft Foundry resource with kind AIServices
questions.explain: A Microsoft Foundry resource is the unified Azure resource boundary for projects and supported AI capabilities. Storage and Search can be connected resources, but neither replaces the Foundry resource or its project and governance boundary.
questions.teach: Azure organises AI work in layers. A resource is the Azure object you create, secure, network and bill. A project sits inside a resource as a workspace for agents, evaluations and files, and connections link in other services such as Search or Storage. Some resource types only host model deployments, while others also bundle the Foundry Tools (Speech, Vision, Language, Content Understanding) and project management in one place.
hints: The requirement is one boundary that covers four things at once: projects, models, agents with evaluations, and the family of Foundry Tools. Look for the option that is described as a unified boundary, not a single-purpose one.

Rule out any option that only hosts model deployments, because it cannot also hold agents and the other tools. Also rule out an option that describes a project with nothing above it, since a project is a child object and needs a parent that owns the security and billing settings.

One option is an older, hub-based way of organising work. The question asks what to create for the current setup, so prefer the resource type that the current architecture is built around over the legacy container.
questions.deep: Storage, Search and Key Vault are connected resources that a project links to; they do not replace the parent resource. Networking, identity and policy are applied at the resource level, so the resource choice decides where you put private endpoints and role assignments. Microsoft Learn: Create a Microsoft Foundry resource, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/multi-service-resource

questions.prompt: A subscription has 240,000 TPM of Standard quota for one model in West Europe. Existing deployments use 160,000 TPM, and a new 100,000-TPM deployment fails quota validation. What is the most direct resolution without changing region or model?
options: Change the deployment to Global Standard while assuming the regional Standard quota automatically transfers
Reduce existing allocations by at least 20,000 TPM or obtain additional quota before creating the deployment
Enable dynamic quota and create the full 100,000-TPM deployment without changing the existing allocations
Create the deployment in another Foundry project that uses the same subscription, model, and regional quota pool
answer: Reduce existing allocations by at least 20,000 TPM or obtain additional quota before creating the deployment
questions.explain: Standard quota is allocated per subscription, region, model, and deployment type. The requested baseline allocations cannot exceed that pool, so quota must be freed from existing deployments or increased first.
questions.teach: Quota is a pool of tokens per minute (TPM) that Azure grants to a subscription for one model, one region and one deployment type. Each deployment you create takes a slice of that pool, and the slices cannot add up to more than the pool. When a new deployment fails validation, the arithmetic is over budget, not the code or the network.
hints: Do the sum first. Add the existing allocations to the new request and compare the total with the pool the subscription holds in that region. The size of the gap is the number the answer has to account for.

The question says to keep the same region and the same model. That removes any answer that works by moving somewhere else or by switching the deployment type and hoping the old allocation follows it, because quota belongs to a specific combination of subscription, region, model and type.

Dynamic quota helps with spikes above an allocation, but it does not let you reserve a baseline that is larger than the pool. Choose the option that respects the size of the pool instead of trying to get around it.
questions.deep: Quota is per subscription, per region, per model and per deployment type, and it is a separate concept from rate limiting on a running deployment. Lowering an existing deployment's TPM returns capacity to the pool; requesting an increase goes through the quota request process. Microsoft Learn: Foundry model quota management, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/quota

questions.prompt: Match each inference requirement to the most appropriate deployment scope or capacity model.
rows: Highest availability when worldwide routing is acceptable
Processing can occur anywhere in the EU data zone, but not outside it
Processing must stay in one specific Azure region
Dedicated capacity and predictable throughput are required
options: Regional deployment
Global deployment
Provisioned throughput
Data Zone deployment
answer: Global deployment
Data Zone deployment
Regional deployment
Provisioned throughput
questions.explain: Global deployments maximize routing flexibility, Data Zone deployments constrain processing to the US or EU zone, and regional deployments constrain it to one region. Provisioned throughput reserves dedicated capacity.
questions.teach: A deployment type answers two questions. Scope: where may a prompt be processed, which is anywhere in Azure (Global), inside a data zone such as the EU or US (Data Zone), or inside one region (Regional). Capacity model: do you share pay-per-token capacity, or reserve dedicated throughput (provisioned)? Scope and capacity model are separate choices that you combine.
hints: Sort the four requirements into two kinds. Three of them are about where processing is allowed to happen. One is about how capacity is bought and guaranteed. Notice which row is the odd one out.

For the location rows, read the boundary closely. One allows worldwide routing, one allows anywhere inside a named zone but nothing outside it, and one pins processing to a single Azure region. The size of the allowed area shrinks from the first to the last.

The row about dedicated capacity and predictable throughput is not about geography at all. It is satisfied by buying reserved throughput, which is a different axis from the three location options. Each option is used once.
questions.deep: Provisioned capacity comes in Global, Data Zone and Regional flavours, so predictable throughput does not by itself settle the residency question. On a real design, state the residency rule first, then pick Standard or Provisioned within that scope. Microsoft Learn: Provisioned throughput for Foundry Models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/concepts/provisioned-throughput

questions.prompt: A new application has bursty and unpredictable traffic, and the team has not yet established a sustained throughput baseline. Which initial deployment approach is most defensible?
options: Reserve the maximum provisioned capacity immediately and disable usage monitoring
Route overflow to an unapproved geography without checking data-residency requirements
Use pay-per-use capacity with quota, throttling, latency, and token monitoring
Create one deployment per user so each request has dedicated throughput
answer: Use pay-per-use capacity with quota, throttling, latency, and token monitoring
questions.explain: A consumption-style deployment plus measurement fits an uncertain bursty workload. Provisioned capacity becomes easier to justify after sustained demand and latency requirements are known and geographic constraints are satisfied.
questions.teach: Capacity is cheapest to plan when demand is known. Pay-per-use (Standard) deployments bill for tokens used and absorb uneven traffic, while provisioned deployments reserve throughput that you pay for whether it is used or not. Without a measured baseline you do not yet know how much to reserve, so teams start flexible and measure.
hints: The stem tells you two facts about the workload: it is bursty and there is no sustained throughput baseline yet. Ask which way of buying capacity is safe when you cannot yet say how much you will need.

Reserving the maximum up front means paying for idle capacity and switching off the numbers that would tell you whether the reservation was needed. Giving every user their own deployment multiplies cost and quota consumption without solving burstiness.

Any answer that sends traffic somewhere without first checking where data may be processed is a residency risk. The defensible option is the one that starts flexible and watches quota, throttling, latency and token use so that a later decision rests on data.
questions.deep: A common path is to start on pay-per-use, collect a few weeks of token and latency data, then move steady baseline traffic to provisioned capacity and keep the bursts on Standard. Reservations make sense once utilisation is predictably high. Microsoft Learn: Provisioned throughput for Foundry Models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/concepts/provisioned-throughput

questions.prompt: Which three changes can reduce inference cost without removing required functionality? Choose three.
options: Remove redundant instructions and retrieved passages while preserving required evidence
Cache generated answers across users without partitioning the cache by identity or authorization context
Truncate every prompt and retrieval result to one fixed size before evaluating whether required evidence is lost
Measure token consumption by feature and enforce explicit budgets, thresholds, or alerts
Route simple, evaluated request classes to a smaller model that meets their quality target
answer: Route simple, evaluated request classes to a smaller model that meets their quality target
Remove redundant instructions and retrieved passages while preserving required evidence
Measure token consumption by feature and enforce explicit budgets, thresholds, or alerts
questions.explain: Right-sizing models, trimming redundant tokens while keeping needed evidence, and measuring token use by feature all lower cost without removing functionality. A shared cache that ignores identity can leak answers between users, and blind truncation can drop evidence the answer needs.
questions.teach: Inference cost is mostly tokens in and tokens out multiplied by a model's price. The levers are therefore choosing a cheaper model where quality allows, sending fewer unnecessary tokens, and measuring where tokens go so that budgets can be enforced. Any cost cut must be checked against quality, and anything shared between users must respect who is allowed to see it.
hints: Treat each option as a change you could make tomorrow and ask two questions: does it really lower token spend, and does it keep the required behaviour intact? A saving that breaks a requirement is not a saving.

Look for two kinds of safe savings: using a smaller model on easy request classes after checking it meets the quality target, and cutting tokens that carry no value, such as repeated instructions, while keeping the evidence the answer needs.

Two options look like savings but carry hidden costs: one shares stored answers across users without any separation, and one cuts everything to a fixed size without checking what is lost. The third correct choice is about knowing where the tokens go before you set limits.
questions.deep: Cost control starts with attribution: tag usage by feature so budgets and alerts point at the real spender. Caching is useful but must be partitioned by identity and authorization context, otherwise it becomes a data-leak path. Microsoft Learn: Foundry Models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/foundry-models/concepts/models-sold-directly-by-azure

questions.prompt: A support app must minimize cost but preserve quality for difficult requests. Which design is best?
options: Route every request to a small model and retry failures with the same model using a longer prompt
Route every request to the largest model and use caching as the only cost-control mechanism
Route solely by prompt character count without evaluating intent complexity or result quality
Route simple intents to a small model, use rules and confidence checks, and escalate complex cases to a more capable model
answer: Route simple intents to a small model, use rules and confidence checks, and escalate complex cases to a more capable model
questions.explain: A bounded routing policy combines lower-cost models and deterministic rules for simple work with a capable fallback for complex or low-confidence cases.
questions.teach: Model routing sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it. A small model plus simple rules covers routine intents, and a more capable model is kept as the fallback for hard or low-confidence cases. The routing policy itself should be tested, like any other part of the system.
hints: The goal has two halves that pull against each other: keep cost low, and keep quality up on the difficult requests. A good design has to serve both halves, so any option that optimises only one is suspect.

Eliminate the extremes. Sending everything to one model, whether the smallest or the largest, gives up either quality or cost. A rule based on a trivial signal such as how long the prompt is says little about how hard the task is.

The remaining option splits traffic by difficulty, uses cheap checks to decide, and has an escalation path when the cheap route is not good enough. That is the shape of a policy that can be measured and tuned.
questions.deep: Routing quality depends on the router. Evaluate it on a labelled set that includes hard cases, and watch the escalation rate in production: if almost everything escalates, the small model is not pulling its weight. Microsoft Learn: Foundry Models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/foundry-models/concepts/models-sold-directly-by-azure

questions.prompt: A document assistant handles many simple classifications and a smaller number of difficult reasoning requests. Which design best balances cost and quality?
options: Use evaluated routing rules to send simple tasks to a suitable small model and escalate complex or low-confidence tasks to a stronger model
Send every request to the small model and escalate only after an HTTP or parsing failure
Send every request to the strongest model and reduce cost by limiting all responses to the same token count
Route by prompt length alone, sending short prompts to the small model and long prompts to the reasoning model
answer: Use evaluated routing rules to send simple tasks to a suitable small model and escalate complex or low-confidence tasks to a stronger model
questions.explain: A measured routing strategy exploits lower-cost models where they meet the quality target and reserves a more capable model for hard cases. Evaluation and fallback criteria keep optimization from silently degrading results.
questions.teach: When a workload mixes many simple tasks with a few hard ones, one model for everything wastes money or hurts quality. Routing rules assign each request to a model, and a fallback catches the cases the cheap route cannot handle. The rules are only trustworthy if they were evaluated against the quality target.
hints: Start from the workload shape: many simple classifications and a smaller number of difficult reasoning requests. The design should spend little on the first group and enough on the second.
Be suspicious of routing signals that are easy to compute but unrelated to difficulty. How long a prompt is, or whether an HTTP error happened, does not tell you whether the answer was good.

Also reject answers that treat cost as a pure output cap. Limiting every response to the same size changes the quality of all answers. The right option names how simple and complex cases are told apart, backed by evaluation and a stronger fallback.
questions.deep: Confidence signals, task classifiers and escalation on validation failure are all legitimate router inputs. Keep a sample of routed traffic under evaluation so that silent quality drops in the cheap path are noticed. Microsoft Learn: Foundry Models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/foundry-models/concepts/models-sold-directly-by-azure

questions.prompt: You need repeatable extraction into a fixed schema. Which generation adjustment is most appropriate?
options: Use the required structured schema but increase temperature to maximize variation in extracted values
Use a low temperature and a constrained structured-output schema
Use JSON mode with a high temperature and validate only that the result parses as JSON
Use a low temperature with prompt examples but accept any object shape the model returns
answer: Use a low temperature and a constrained structured-output schema
questions.explain: Low randomness and schema-constrained output support deterministic extraction. The application should also validate the returned structure.
questions.teach: Temperature controls how random token choice is: low values make output more repeatable, high values make it more varied. Structured output constrains the reply to a declared schema so that field names and types are guaranteed. For extraction into a fixed layout you usually want both repeatability and a guaranteed shape, and you still validate in code.
hints: The need is repeatable extraction into a fixed schema. Split that into two separate requirements: the same input should give the same values, and the output must always have the same shape.

Ask which setting influences repeatability and which setting influences shape. An option that fixes only one of the two leaves the other to chance, and an option that raises randomness works against the first requirement.
A mode that only guarantees the text is valid JSON does not guarantee your field names or types. Look for the option that pairs the settings that address both requirements.
questions.deep: Structured outputs with a strict JSON schema constrain generation to your schema, while JSON mode only guarantees syntactically valid JSON. Low temperature reduces variance but does not make a model deterministic, so validation and tests still matter. Microsoft Learn: Structured outputs with Azure OpenAI, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/structured-outputs

questions.prompt: Match each model API error to the most appropriate first remediation.
rows: DeploymentNotFound
401 Unauthorized
429 Too Many Requests
options: Apply a bounded exponential-backoff retry policy
Verify the credential and endpoint authentication configuration
Verify the configured deployment name
answer: Verify the configured deployment name
Verify the credential and endpoint authentication configuration
Apply a bounded exponential-backoff retry policy
questions.explain: DeploymentNotFound usually means the deployment name is absent or misspelled, 401 indicates missing or invalid authentication, and 429 indicates rate limiting that should be handled with a controlled backoff policy.
questions.teach: Error codes are a first diagnostic. A 401 means the caller could not be authenticated, so credentials or endpoint authentication settings are wrong. A not-found style error on a deployment points at a name that does not exist. A 429 means the service is throttling, which is a transient condition handled by waiting and retrying politely.
hints: Translate each error into plain words first. One says the thing you asked for was not found, one says the service does not know who you are, and one says you are asking too often.

Pick the remediation that attacks the cause in each phrase. A missing-thing error is fixed by checking the name or identifier you used, and an unknown-caller error is fixed by checking how you sign in and where you send the request.

For the too-many-requests error, a repair that changes your configuration is not needed. The correct first step is to slow down in a controlled way and try again, with limits on how many attempts you make.
questions.deep: Never retry a 401 or a not-found error blindly, since the same request will fail the same way. Retries belong to transient failures, with a cap, exponential backoff and jitter, and respect for any Retry-After header. Microsoft Learn: Azure OpenAI image generation models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/dall-e

questions.prompt: Which release process best reduces the risk of a prompt or model update reaching production?
options: Edit the production prompt in the portal, export it afterward, and compare a small sample manually
Run the evaluation gate in test but allow operators to change the production prompt and index configuration manually
Version configuration as code, deploy to a test environment, run quality and safety evaluations, and require a gated promotion
Promote the newest model automatically, then run the representative evaluation set against production traffic
answer: Version configuration as code, deploy to a test environment, run quality and safety evaluations, and require a gated promotion
questions.explain: Versioned configuration, repeatable deployment, evaluation gates, and controlled promotion make changes testable and reversible before they affect production users.
questions.teach: AI changes are code changes. A prompt, a model version or a search index setting can change behaviour as much as a code edit, so they belong in version control and should move through the same pipeline: deploy to a test environment, run repeatable evaluations, and promote only if the results pass a gate.
hints: Imagine the change reaching real users. The safest process finds problems before that moment, can be repeated, and leaves a record of what changed. Judge each option by whether it gives you those three things.
Be wary of any process where a person edits production directly or where production traffic is used as the first test. Both skip the repeatable check that an automated evaluation provides.
Look for the option that treats prompts and configuration like source code, tests them in a separate environment against quality and safety measures, and makes promotion depend on the result.
questions.deep: Evaluation gates should run on a representative, versioned dataset, with thresholds agreed in advance, so a pass or fail is not argued after the fact. Pair the gate with a rollback path to the last known good version. Microsoft Learn: Cloud evaluation with the Microsoft Foundry SDK, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/how-to/develop/cloud-evaluation

questions.prompt: Which four release controls best reduce risk when promoting a new prompt, model version, and retrieval configuration? Choose four.
options: Run the pipeline evaluation but allow unversioned prompt and index changes directly in the production portal
Use a staged or canary deployment with monitored acceptance thresholds
Run repeatable quality, groundedness, and safety evaluations on a representative dataset
Version the prompt, model deployment settings, and index schema with the application
Retain a tested rollback path to the previous workflow version
Deploy the change to all production traffic before running the representative regression dataset
answer: Version the prompt, model deployment settings, and index schema with the application
Run repeatable quality, groundedness, and safety evaluations on a representative dataset
Use a staged or canary deployment with monitored acceptance thresholds
Retain a tested rollback path to the previous workflow version
questions.explain: Versioned artefacts, repeatable quality and safety evaluations, staged or canary exposure with acceptance thresholds, and a tested rollback path together make a controlled release. Running the regression set only after full rollout, or allowing unversioned production edits, removes the early warning and the reproducibility.
questions.teach: Releasing an AI change safely uses the same controls as any production release plus evaluation. Version the artefacts that define behaviour (prompt, model settings, index schema), measure quality and safety on a representative dataset, expose the change gradually, and keep a tested way back.
hints: The stem asks for four controls that lower risk when a prompt, a model version and a retrieval configuration change together. Look for controls that act before, during and after exposure to users.
Before exposure: what lets you reproduce exactly what was released, and what proves quality and safety on a test set? Two of the correct options sit here.

During and after exposure: how do you limit the number of users who see a bad change, and how do you undo it quickly? Reject any option that tests only after everything is already live, or that lets people change production settings outside the pipeline.
questions.deep: Canary exposure is only useful with monitored acceptance thresholds, such as groundedness, safety and latency, that trigger an automatic hold or rollback. Keep the previous prompt, deployment and index version available until the new one is proven. Microsoft Learn: Cloud evaluation with the Microsoft Foundry SDK, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/how-to/develop/cloud-evaluation

questions.prompt: A workflow capability is documented as preview. The application must meet a production SLA. What is the most appropriate release decision?
options: Copy the preview API schema into the application so future service changes cannot affect it
Remove all evaluation because preview features cannot be measured
Treat preview and generally available features as equivalent when both appear in the portal
Record the preview status, validate limitations, and require an explicit risk decision before production use
answer: Record the preview status, validate limitations, and require an explicit risk decision before production use
questions.explain: Preview status is a lifecycle and support constraint. It should be captured with the design, validated against requirements, and accepted explicitly rather than being inferred from portal availability or hidden by copied schemas.
questions.teach: Cloud features move through lifecycle stages such as preview and general availability. Preview features may change, can have limited support or no service-level agreement, and may be removed. Using one in production is a risk decision that should be recorded and justified, not a default.
hints: Ask what preview status actually tells you: the feature may change, may carry weaker support terms, and may not be covered by the availability promise the application needs.

Reject answers that pretend the stage does not matter, such as treating preview and general availability as equal because both appear in the portal. Also reject answers that jump to an extreme, like dropping measurement altogether.

A frozen copy of an API schema does not protect you from service-side changes. The mature answer makes the status visible, checks the known limits against your requirements, and has someone accept the risk on the record before launch.
questions.deep: Record lifecycle status next to each dependency in the design document and re-check it before every release, because a feature can move to GA, change shape or be retired. The Learn page for the feature states its current stage. This was a preview feature when the source bank was checked, so confirm its current status on Microsoft Learn before relying on it. Microsoft Learn: Foundry workflows (preview), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/workflow

questions.prompt: A container app must call a Foundry project endpoint in production. Which authentication design is preferred?
options: Use its managed identity through DefaultAzureCredential and assign only the required role
Use the project's API key stored in Key Vault and retrieve it through the container's managed identity
Use an interactive developer credential in production and restrict access through conditional access
Use a client secret stored in Key Vault and rotate it through the deployment pipeline
answer: Use its managed identity through DefaultAzureCredential and assign only the required role
questions.explain: Managed identity removes stored credentials. DefaultAzureCredential selects it in Azure, and RBAC should grant only the data-plane permissions the workload needs.
questions.teach: A workload running in Azure can be given its own identity, so no password or key has to be stored anywhere. The Azure Identity library hides the details: DefaultAzureCredential tries a chain of sources and, in Azure hosting, picks up the workload's managed identity. What that identity may do is then set by role assignments, and the safest assignment is the smallest role at the smallest scope.
hints: The preferred design is the one with no secret to store, rotate or leak. Sort the options into those that still depend on some stored credential and those that rely on an identity assigned to the workload itself.

Storing a secret in a vault is better than hard-coding it, but it is still a secret that must be created, rotated and fetched. An interactive developer sign-in is built for people at a keyboard and does not belong on a production service.
Once the identity is chosen, the second half of the answer is about authorization. Prefer the option that grants only the permissions the call actually needs rather than a broad role.
questions.deep: DefaultAzureCredential is convenient in development, but in production you can pin ManagedIdentityCredential to avoid probing several sources. If a role assignment was just made, allow a few minutes for propagation before concluding it is wrong. Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Foundry architecture, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/architecture

questions.prompt: A Python application successfully obtains a Microsoft Entra token for https://ai.azure.com/.default, but a Foundry request returns HTTP 403. What should the team check first?
options: Whether the principal has Reader at the project scope but no Foundry data-plane role
Whether the calling principal has the required RBAC role at the resource or project scope
Whether the principal has Search Index Data Reader only on the connected search service
Whether the same token should instead use the Azure Resource Manager audience for the project request
answer: Whether the calling principal has the required RBAC role at the resource or project scope
questions.explain: A valid token proves authentication, while HTTP 403 commonly indicates that authorization is missing. The principal needs the appropriate Foundry data-plane role at a scope that contains the requested project or resource operation.
questions.teach: Authentication and authorization fail in different ways. Authentication proves who the caller is and, when it fails, usually returns 401. Authorization decides what that caller may do and, when it fails for a valid caller, usually returns 403. A caller that already has a good token and still gets a 403 has a permissions problem, not a token problem.
hints: Start from what the facts prove. The application already obtained a Microsoft Entra token for the right audience, so the question is no longer who the caller is. Think about what comes after identity.

A 403 on a valid token means the service understood who called and refused the request. Ask which setting on the Azure side controls what a known principal is allowed to do, and at which levels of the hierarchy it can be set.

Be careful with roles that sound close but grant only management-plane visibility, and with roles on a different service entirely. The check should be about whether a data-plane role exists that covers the project or resource being called.
questions.deep: Reader on a resource is a control-plane role and does not grant data actions. When troubleshooting, check the role at the project and at the parent resource, remember assignments inherit downward, and allow time for new assignments to propagate. Microsoft Learn: Authentication and authorization in Microsoft Foundry, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/authentication-authorization-foundry

questions.prompt: Several projects in the same Foundry resource must reuse an approved Azure AI Search connection. Project teams must not gain permission to administer unrelated resources. Which design is best?
options: Create one resource-level key connection and give every project team Foundry Owner so they can resolve and edit it
Create a managed-identity connection in every project and let the central team update each copy independently
Create the reusable connection at the Foundry resource boundary and grant each project team only its required project and target-resource data access
Create an equivalent project-level connection in every project and give each team Contributor on the Foundry resource
answer: Create the reusable connection at the Foundry resource boundary and grant each project team only its required project and target-resource data access
questions.explain: Create the reusable connection once at the Foundry resource boundary, then give each project team only its project role and the data access it needs on the target resource. Copies per project, Owner or Contributor on the whole resource, and independently edited managed-identity copies all defeat central control or least privilege.
questions.teach: A connection stores how a Foundry project reaches another service, such as Azure AI Search. A connection can live at the Foundry resource level, where several projects can reuse it, or inside a single project. Reuse reduces duplicates, and role assignments decide who can edit the connection and who can only use what it points to.
hints: There are two requirements to satisfy together: several projects must reuse one approved connection, and the project teams must not gain rights over unrelated resources. Test each option against both.

Copying the same connection into every project defeats the idea of one approved definition and makes updates harder. Any option that hands out Owner or Contributor on the whole resource gives far more than a project team needs.
Look for the design that creates the connection once at the shared level and then grants each team only access scoped to its own project and to the data it must read.
questions.deep: A connection is not a permission: the identity that actually calls Search still needs a role on the Search service. Separating who administers a connection from who uses it is the point of resource-level sharing. Microsoft Learn: Add a connection to a Foundry project, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/how-to/connections-add

questions.prompt: A signed URL must give one reviewer read access to a claim image for 15 minutes. Policy prohibits signing with a Storage account key. What should the application issue?
options: An account SAS signed with the Storage account key and limited to Blob service read access
A service SAS signed with the Storage account key and limited to read access for 15 minutes
A Microsoft Entra bearer token copied into the URL for the reviewer to reuse during the 15-minute period
A user delegation SAS authorized with Microsoft Entra credentials
answer: A user delegation SAS authorized with Microsoft Entra credentials
questions.explain: A user delegation SAS is secured with Microsoft Entra credentials instead of the Storage account key and can be constrained to the required resource, permission, and short expiry. It is the recommended SAS type when supported.
questions.teach: A shared access signature (SAS) is a URL that carries limited, time-boxed access to storage. There are three kinds. An account SAS and a service SAS are signed with the storage account key. A user delegation SAS is signed with a key obtained using Microsoft Entra credentials, so the account key is never used and access can be audited per identity.
hints: Two facts decide this one: the access must expire after 15 minutes and be limited to reading one image, and the policy forbids signing with the storage account key. Underline the second fact.
Check each option for what it is signed with. Anything signed with the account key breaks the policy, no matter how narrow its permissions or how short its lifetime.

A bearer token is a credential for the Authorization header, not something to paste into a URL and hand to someone else. The right answer is a URL-based signature whose signing material comes from Microsoft Entra.
questions.deep: A user delegation SAS can be revoked by revoking the delegation key, and it is the Microsoft-recommended SAS type when supported. Keep the lifetime short and the permission set minimal, because a SAS is a bearer link that anyone holding it can use. Microsoft Learn: Shared access signatures for Azure Storage, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-sas-overview

questions.prompt: Continuous evaluation rules fail with authorization errors even though an engineer can view the project. Which identity should receive the documented project role required to run the rules?
options: The Foundry project's managed identity at the project or required resource scope
The model deployment's service principal at tenant scope
Every engineer's personal identity at subscription scope
The browser session identity stored as a project connection secret
answer: The Foundry project's managed identity at the project or required resource scope
questions.explain: Continuous evaluation uses the project managed identity to perform its work. Grant that workload identity the documented Foundry project role at the narrowest required scope instead of widening human or tenant permissions.
questions.teach: Some Foundry features run in the background on your behalf, such as scheduled or continuous evaluation. Background work cannot use an engineer's browser session, so it runs as the project's own managed identity. If that identity lacks the required role, the feature fails with authorization errors even when people can see everything in the portal.
hints: The clue is that a human engineer can view the project but the rules still fail. That tells you the failing caller is not the engineer. Ask who actually performs the work when no person is clicking.

A feature that runs on a schedule needs an identity that exists independently of any signed-in person. Granting rights to every engineer or to a distant tenant-wide principal widens access without fixing the real caller.
Choose the option that gives the documented role to the workload identity that belongs to the project, at the narrowest scope that covers the work.
questions.deep: Background features act as the project's own managed identity, so the documented role belongs on that identity at the narrowest scope that covers the work. When a background job fails with 403 while portal access works, check the identity that executes it first. Microsoft Learn: Agent Monitoring Dashboard, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/observability/how-to/how-to-monitor-agents-dashboard?view=foundry

questions.prompt: An application subnet can route to a Foundry private endpoint, but the service hostname still resolves to its public address. What is missing?
options: A larger model quota in the private endpoint region
Private DNS configuration linked to the virtual network
A semantic ranker attached to the Foundry project
An API key stored in the subnet's route table
answer: Private DNS configuration linked to the virtual network
questions.explain: Private endpoint traffic depends on name resolution mapping the service hostname to the endpoint's private address. Routing alone does not rewrite DNS, and credentials or model quota cannot correct the resolved destination.
questions.teach: A private endpoint gives a service a private IP address inside your virtual network. Clients still use the service's normal hostname, so name resolution must return the private address instead of the public one. That is done with a private DNS zone linked to the network. Routing alone does not change what a hostname resolves to.
hints: Read the symptom precisely: traffic can be routed to the private endpoint, but the hostname resolves to a public address. The connection path exists, so the problem sits in how the name is turned into an address.
Eliminate options that have nothing to do with name resolution. Model quota, credentials in a route table and ranking features do not influence which IP address a hostname maps to.
Think about which Azure object maps a service hostname to a private address and which link makes the application's network use it.
questions.deep: Typical failures: the private DNS zone is missing, is not linked to the virtual network, or an on-premises resolver does not forward the privatelink zone. Test with nslookup from inside the network and expect a private address. Microsoft Learn: Authentication and authorization in Microsoft Foundry, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/authentication-authorization-foundry

questions.prompt: An agent can read inventory and submit purchase orders. Which two controls most directly reduce the impact of an erroneous tool call? Choose two.
options: Give the agent a narrow order schema and credentials limited to the required operations
Place the purchase-order API key in the system prompt so the model can verify it
Give every agent Contributor so a failed call can repair its own permissions
Require approval before the state-changing submission while allowing read-only lookup without that approval
answer: Give the agent a narrow order schema and credentials limited to the required operations
Require approval before the state-changing submission while allowing read-only lookup without that approval
questions.explain: A narrow schema and least-privilege credential bound what the tool can do, while approval gates the consequential action. Broad roles and secrets in prompts increase both accidental and adversarial impact.
questions.teach: An agent that can call tools can also call them wrongly. You cannot make the model infallible, so you limit the damage of a wrong call. Two controls do most of the work: give the tool a narrow contract and a credential that can do only what the tool needs, and put a human approval in front of any action that changes state while leaving harmless reads free.
hints: Ask for each option whether it would shrink the impact of a mistaken call or make mistakes worse. You want controls that reduce blast radius, not ones that widen it.

One group of options concerns what the agent is able to do at all: how narrow the interface is and how limited the credential is. Another group concerns when a person must say yes. Pick one strong control from each group.
Discard any option that gives an agent more power in the hope it can fix its own errors, and any option that puts a secret where the model can read it.
questions.deep: Allow read-only lookups without friction and gate only side-effecting calls, otherwise approvals become noise that people click through. Never place credentials in prompts, since prompt content can leak or be echoed back by the model. Microsoft Learn: OpenAPI tools for Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/tools/openapi

questions.prompt: Which three controls most directly limit the blast radius of an autonomous operations agent? Choose three.
options: Allowlist narrowly scoped tools and identities
Require approval for destructive or high-impact actions
Use narrow tools but let the model treat a high confidence score as authorization for destructive calls
Give the agent broad tools and credentials but require human approval before every read and write call
Enforce argument validation, policy checks, and execution limits outside the model
answer: Allowlist narrowly scoped tools and identities
Require approval for destructive or high-impact actions
Enforce argument validation, policy checks, and execution limits outside the model
questions.explain: Least-privilege tools, explicit approvals, and deterministic enforcement outside the model constrain impact. Model confidence is not an authorization control.
questions.teach: Blast radius is how much damage a system can do when it misbehaves. For an autonomous agent you cap it with deterministic controls outside the model: only the tools and identities it needs, approvals for high-impact steps, and server-side checks of arguments and limits. The model's confidence is not a control, because a model can be confidently wrong.
hints: The stem asks for controls that directly limit how much harm an autonomous agent can cause. Separate options that make the agent less capable of harm from options that merely give the impression of oversight.
Three of the correct controls fit three layers: what the agent is allowed to reach, which actions need a human, and what is enforced in code that the model cannot talk its way around.

Be suspicious of an option that gives broad access and then asks a human to approve every single call, which defeats itself, and of any option that treats a model's own confidence score as permission.
questions.deep: Policy checks must live outside the model, in the tool layer or a gateway, so that a prompt injection cannot change them. Combine allowlists, approval gates and execution limits such as rate and spend caps. This was a preview feature when the source bank was checked, so confirm its current status on Microsoft Learn before relying on it. Microsoft Learn: Foundry workflows, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/workflow

questions.prompt: The app must detect jailbreak attempts, classify harmful text and images, and detect agent tool use that is premature or misaligned with the user's request. Which three Content Safety capabilities directly address the described risks? Choose three.
options: Groundedness detection for comparing generated answers with supplied source material
Protected-material detection for identifying known text or code in generated output
Analyze Text and Analyze Image APIs for harm-category severity classification
Task adherence checks for agent tool calls that may be misaligned or premature
Prompt Shields for direct user-prompt attacks and indirect attacks in documents
answer: Prompt Shields for direct user-prompt attacks and indirect attacks in documents
Analyze Text and Analyze Image APIs for harm-category severity classification
Task adherence checks for agent tool calls that may be misaligned or premature
questions.explain: Prompt Shields detects prompt attacks, the text and image analysis APIs classify harm categories by severity, and task adherence evaluates whether an agent's tool use is premature or misaligned with the request. Groundedness detection and protected-material detection answer other questions that the scenario does not raise.
questions.teach: Azure AI Content Safety bundles several detectors that answer different questions. Some classify harmful content by category and severity, some detect attempts to manipulate the model through the user prompt or through documents, some compare an answer with source material, and some check whether an agent's tool use fits what the user asked. Pick the detector that matches the risk named in the scenario.
hints: Write the three risks from the scenario as three questions: is someone trying to jailbreak the model, is the content itself harmful, and is the agent doing something the user did not ask for? Each question has its own capability.

Match each risk to the detector that is built for it. Be careful with capabilities that sound related but answer a different question, such as checking an answer against supplied sources or finding known protected text.
Two options can be ruled out because their purpose is not among the three risks described. Choose the three that cover the three named needs.
questions.deep: Layer the detectors: Prompt Shields at input, harm classification on input and output, and task adherence around tool calls. Each has its own thresholds and response codes, so decide in advance what the application does on a detection. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Content Safety overview, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-safety/overview

questions.prompt: Match each risk to the most directly applicable Azure AI Content Safety capability.
rows: A user tries to override the system message
A retrieved document contains hidden instructions for the model
An uploaded image might contain configured harm categories
An agent attempts a tool action that is premature or misaligned with the user's task
options: Prompt Shields document analysis
Task adherence detection
Analyze Image
Prompt Shields user-prompt analysis
answer: Prompt Shields user-prompt analysis
Prompt Shields document analysis
Analyze Image
Task adherence detection
questions.explain: Prompt Shields distinguishes attacks in user prompts from attacks in supplied documents. Analyze Image classifies visual harms, while task adherence evaluates whether proposed agent tool use aligns with the interaction.
questions.teach: Content Safety separates where an attack comes from. A user prompt attack tries to override the system message directly, while an indirect attack hides instructions inside documents or tool results that the model reads. They are analysed separately. Harm classification works on text or images, and task adherence looks at an agent's proposed tool actions.
hints: Read each risk for where the bad content appears: typed by the user, buried in something retrieved, inside a picture, or in the agent's own plan. Four places, four tools.

Two rows involve instructions aimed at the model. One arrives from the person chatting, and one arrives from a document the model was given. The same product handles both, but through two different analysis modes.

The row about an uploaded picture needs the capability that scores visual harm categories. The row about a premature or off-task action needs the capability that compares planned tool calls with the user's intent. Each option is used once.
questions.deep: Document analysis is the defence for indirect injection, where text from a web page, PDF or email tries to act as an instruction. Run it on untrusted grounding content before that content reaches the model. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Content Safety overview, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-safety/overview

questions.prompt: A team must tune harm-category thresholds while minimizing both unsafe output and unnecessary blocking. What should it do?
options: Tune thresholds only on adversarial examples and use the setting with the highest block rate
Set every category to the most restrictive threshold without testing normal business content
Evaluate candidate thresholds on representative adversarial and normal datasets, then monitor block and safety rates
Use the service defaults permanently and monitor only the number of requests that receive HTTP errors
answer: Evaluate candidate thresholds on representative adversarial and normal datasets, then monitor block and safety rates
questions.explain: Safety policy tuning is an empirical tradeoff. Representative evaluation and production monitoring reveal false positives and missed harms; no single threshold provides an absolute safety guarantee.
questions.teach: Safety thresholds are a trade-off. A very strict setting blocks more harmful output but also blocks legitimate business content, and a loose setting does the reverse. No threshold guarantees safety, so the sound method is empirical: try candidate settings on test data that represents both attacks and ordinary traffic, then keep measuring in production.
hints: The stem asks you to reduce two kinds of mistake together: unsafe output that slips through and legitimate content that gets blocked. Any answer that looks at only one kind of mistake is incomplete.
Settings tuned only on attacks look great on attacks and can wreck normal use. Settings chosen as the strictest possible, without testing normal content, will block real work.
Look for the option that tests on data containing both adversarial and normal examples and keeps watching block rates and safety outcomes after release.
questions.deep: Review a sample of blocked and allowed items regularly to estimate false positives and false negatives. Defaults are a starting point for tuning, not a permanent answer, and you should log decisions so changes can be audited. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Content Safety overview, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-safety/overview

questions.prompt: Prompt Shields returns documentsAnalysis[2].attackDetected = true for one retrieved passage. What should a grounded agent do?
options: Move the passage into the system-message section so its instructions are evaluated at a higher priority
Quarantine the passage but send an automatically generated summary of it to the agent as trusted context
Keep the passage when a normal harm-category analysis returns low severity after the Prompt Shields detection
Exclude or block that passage, record the event, and continue only with trusted evidence under the application's policy
answer: Exclude or block that passage, record the event, and continue only with trusted evidence under the application's policy
questions.explain: A detected document attack identifies untrusted grounding content that may be trying to redirect the model. The application should enforce its block or exclusion policy and retain an audit event; Prompt Shields does not replace other safety controls.
questions.teach: Prompt Shields can analyse documents that you intend to give to a model. If it flags one with attackDetected set to true, that document is untrusted input that may be trying to redirect the model. Applications decide what to do on a detection, and the safe default is to keep the flagged text away from the model and record that it happened.
hints: Treat the detection as a finding about the content, not about the user. The field says an attack was detected in one retrieved passage, so ask what you would do with a document you now know is hostile.

Several options look like clever ways to keep using the passage: summarising it, trusting it because another score is low, or promoting it to a higher-priority place in the prompt. Ask whether any of these removes the risk or only hides it.
The answer keeps hostile text out of the model's context, leaves an audit trail, and continues with evidence that is still trusted.
questions.deep: A low harm score does not cancel an attack finding, since harm classification and attack detection are different checks. Never move untrusted text into the system message: higher-priority placement makes an injection more powerful, not safer. Microsoft Learn: Prompt Shields quickstart, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-safety/quickstart-jailbreak

questions.prompt: Which three records make an agent action most reproducible during an audit? Choose three.
options: The generated recommendation and model confidence without retrieved evidence or tool arguments
Hourly aggregate latency, token, and error metrics without operation-level correlation
Retrieved document and chunk identifiers together with the effective search-index version
The model name plus the exact deployment and workflow versions used for the run
The tool name, server-validated arguments, result identifier, and execution status
answer: The model name plus the exact deployment and workflow versions used for the run
The tool name, server-validated arguments, result identifier, and execution status
Retrieved document and chunk identifiers together with the effective search-index version
questions.explain: Model, deployment and workflow versions, the tool name with validated arguments, result identifier and status, and the retrieved document and chunk identifiers with the index version together explain what inputs and operations produced an outcome. Hourly aggregates or an outcome without its evidence cannot reproduce the decision path.
questions.teach: An action is reproducible when you can reconstruct what produced it. For an agent that means three things: which model, deployment and workflow version ran, what the tool call did and with which arguments and result, and which pieces of retrieved evidence were in front of the model, including the version of the index they came from. Totals and summaries cannot replay a decision.
hints: Ask what you would need in order to rerun or explain one specific agent action next month. A good audit record answers: who or what ran it, what it did, and what it saw.
Be wary of options that keep only aggregates, such as hourly metrics, or only the outcome, such as the final recommendation. Those say that something happened but not how.
The three correct records line up with the three questions: the identity and version of the run, the details of each tool call, and the retrieval provenance including which index version supplied it.
questions.deep: Store identifiers rather than full content where the content is sensitive, and keep them in the same trace so one correlation ID joins retrieval, model and tool records. Index versioning matters because the same query returns different chunks after a re-ingest. Microsoft Learn: Foundry agent tracing, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/observability/how-to/trace-agent-setup

questions.prompt: Which four signal groups should a production RAG agent dashboard include? Choose four.
options: Search-index freshness, ingestion health, and retrieval-quality measurements
End-to-end and component latency, token consumption, retry, and throttling signals
Only overall endpoint availability and request volume, without retrieval or model-quality telemetry
Safety-filter events and rates broken down by the applicable risk categories
Groundedness and answer-relevance measurements from a representative evaluation set
answer: Groundedness and answer-relevance measurements from a representative evaluation set
Search-index freshness, ingestion health, and retrieval-quality measurements
Safety-filter events and rates broken down by the applicable risk categories
End-to-end and component latency, token consumption, retry, and throttling signals
questions.explain: A production view needs quality, retrieval, safety, and operational signals. Together they separate model problems from poor evidence, safety incidents, and capacity or latency issues.
questions.teach: A production RAG agent can fail in several separate ways: the answer can be ungrounded, the retrieval can be stale or poor, the output can be unsafe, or the system can be slow, throttled or costly. A dashboard that shows only one of those groups cannot tell you which kind of failure you are looking at, so it needs signals from each.
hints: List the ways a RAG agent can go wrong, then ask which measurement would reveal each. Quality of the answer, quality and freshness of what was retrieved, safety, and plain operations are different families.
A dashboard with only uptime and request counts says the service is alive but not whether its answers are good. Look for the option that is clearly too narrow and set it aside.
The four correct groups together let you separate a model problem from a poor-evidence problem, a safety incident and a capacity problem.
questions.deep: Plot evaluation scores per release so a drop lines up with a change, and alert on index freshness separately from answer quality.
