Safety-filter rates are best broken down by category so a spike points to a specific risk. Microsoft Learn: Cloud evaluation with the Microsoft Foundry SDK, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/how-to/develop/cloud-evaluation

questions.prompt: Which four signals belong on an operational dashboard for a RAG ingestion and search pipeline? Choose four.
options: Document freshness, indexed counts, and delay in processing updates or deletions
Retrieval relevance measured repeatedly against a stable representative query set
Model-deployment quota and token utilization without ingestion or retrieval measurements
Embedding coverage plus vector dimension, generation, and field-mapping failures
Indexer completion status, failed documents, and detailed enrichment-skill errors
Portal availability and administrator sign-in counts without document or query quality signals
answer: Indexer completion status, failed documents, and detailed enrichment-skill errors
Document freshness, indexed counts, and delay in processing updates or deletions
Embedding coverage plus vector dimension, generation, and field-mapping failures
Retrieval relevance measured repeatedly against a stable representative query set
questions.explain: A pipeline dashboard needs indexer status and enrichment errors, document freshness and processing delay, embedding coverage and vector-field health, and retrieval relevance measured repeatedly on a stable query set. Quota or token data on its own, and portal availability, do not show whether the indexed evidence is current or relevant.
questions.teach: A search-based RAG system has an ingestion half and a query half. The ingestion half can quietly fail: documents error out in an enrichment skill, updates arrive late, deletions are not applied, or embeddings are missing. The query half can quietly degrade in relevance. An operational dashboard must show both halves, not only the health of the model endpoint.
hints: Split the pipeline into what happens before a user searches and what happens when they do. The stem asks for signals for the ingestion and search pipeline, so look for ones about both halves.

Some options measure things next to the pipeline, such as model quota or portal sign-ins. They may be useful elsewhere but do not tell you whether the indexed evidence is complete, current or relevant.

The right four cover: whether indexer runs succeed, whether content is fresh and counts match, whether every chunk has a valid vector, and whether retrieval quality stays steady on a fixed set of queries.
questions.deep: Use a stable, representative query set with known good results to detect relevance regressions after schema, skill or embedding changes. Track deletion lag too: an expired document that stays searchable is a correctness and compliance bug. Microsoft Learn: Monitor Azure AI Search, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-monitor-usage

questions.prompt: An agent passed its preproduction evaluation, but the team now needs quality and safety scores for a configurable sample of real production interactions. What should the team configure?
options: Continuous evaluation for the deployed agent and its production traffic
A scheduled red-team scan with production sampling disabled
Distributed tracing with every span treated as an evaluation score
A larger local test dataset that is run manually after each incident
answer: Continuous evaluation for the deployed agent and its production traffic
questions.explain: Continuous evaluation samples deployed interactions and applies configured evaluators so quality and safety can be monitored over time. Traces provide diagnostic evidence, but a trace alone is not an evaluation score.
questions.teach: Pre-production evaluation tests a fixed dataset before release. Production behaviour differs, because real users ask things the test set never contained. Continuous evaluation samples real interactions from a deployed agent and scores them with the evaluators you configure, so quality and safety can be tracked over time.
hints: The agent already passed its tests before release. The new need is about real interactions after release, scored for quality and safety, using only a sample of traffic.
Split the options into those that run once on a prepared dataset or by hand and those that watch live traffic continuously. The need clearly sits in the second group.
Beware of options that sound like measurement but are not scores: a trace shows what happened inside a request, but a score needs an evaluator that judges the result.
questions.deep: Sampling rate is a cost-versus-coverage knob, and continuous evaluation needs a deployed agent plus the permissions described in the Foundry monitoring guidance. Pair it with alerts on score drops so someone reacts. Microsoft Learn: Evaluate Microsoft Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/observability/how-to/evaluate-agent

questions.prompt: A groundedness score drops after a release. Which combination best supports both detection and root-cause analysis?
options: Token-count alerts to detect the score change and model temperature to identify the failing document
Continuous evaluation to detect the score change and correlated traces to inspect retrieval and tool spans
Search replicas to calculate groundedness and quota metrics to reconstruct prompts
A content filter to calculate relevance and a deployment name to reconstruct tool arguments
answer: Continuous evaluation to detect the score change and correlated traces to inspect retrieval and tool spans
questions.explain: Evaluation measures response qualities such as groundedness, while correlated traces expose the retrieval, model, and tool operations that produced an interaction. The two signals answer different but complementary questions.
questions.teach: Evaluation and tracing answer different questions. An evaluator turns an interaction into a score, such as groundedness, so you can see that quality changed. A trace records the operations inside an interaction, such as retrieval, model calls and tool calls, so you can see why. Detecting a regression and finding its cause usually need both.
hints: Break the scenario into two jobs: notice that a quality score fell after a release, and work out which part of the run caused it. Ask which kind of tool does each job.
A tool that produces a quality score cannot also tell you which retrieval step misbehaved, and a tool that shows internal steps does not by itself compute a score. They complement each other.
Discard options that assign a job to something unrelated, such as a search replica, a content filter or a deployment name. Those do not calculate groundedness or reconstruct arguments.
questions.deep: Link both signals with a shared operation ID so a low-scoring interaction can be opened as a trace. Compare traces from before and after the release for the same prompts to isolate what changed. Microsoft Learn: Evaluate Microsoft Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/observability/how-to/evaluate-agent

questions.prompt: Which two records are most important for reproducing and auditing an approved generated asset? Choose two.
options: Only the current model catalog entry, even if the asset used an older deployment
Only the final file size and the reviewer's display name
The source-asset identifiers, prompt, and approval decision
The exact model deployment or version and generation parameters
answer: The exact model deployment or version and generation parameters
The source-asset identifiers, prompt, and approval decision
questions.explain: Reproducible provenance connects the output to its exact model/deployment, inputs, parameters, source assets, safety results, and approval. Current catalog metadata or superficial file properties cannot reconstruct an earlier generation.
questions.teach: To reproduce or audit a generated asset you must be able to say exactly how it was made. That means the precise model deployment and version, the settings used for generation, the inputs that fed it (source assets and prompt), and the decision by which it was approved. Facts that can change later, or that describe the file superficially, do not recreate the original run.
hints: Imagine someone asks six months later how this exact image was produced and who allowed it out. List what you would need to rebuild that story.

A file's size, a reviewer's display name, or a description of the current catalogue say nothing about how the asset was made. The catalogue also moves on, so it may no longer match the deployment that was used.
The two useful records pair up: how the generator was configured, and what went in and who approved the result.
questions.deep: Record the deployment name and model version, not just the model family, because behaviour changes between versions. Link the safety results and the approval event to the same asset ID so an audit can follow one thread. Microsoft Learn: Set up tracing for Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/observability/how-to/trace-agent-setup

questions.prompt: Arrange the activities in the most defensible order for releasing a changed agent.
tray: Compare results with thresholds and approve or reject the candidate
Build or update a representative labeled evaluation dataset
Run quality, safety, and tool-behavior evaluations against the candidate
Deploy the approved version and continuously evaluate sampled production traffic
answer: Build or update a representative labeled evaluation dataset
Run quality, safety, and tool-behavior evaluations against the candidate
Compare results with thresholds and approve or reject the candidate
Deploy the approved version and continuously evaluate sampled production traffic
questions.explain: A representative dataset precedes evaluation, evaluation evidence informs the release gate, and production monitoring begins only after the approved candidate is deployed. Reversing the order turns production users into the test set.
questions.teach: A safe agent release follows evidence. First you need test data that represents real use, then you run evaluations against the candidate version, then you compare the scores with agreed thresholds and decide, and only after approval do you deploy and watch real traffic. Doing the steps out of order turns production users into the test set.
hints: Ask what each step needs as input. You cannot score a candidate without something to score it on, and you cannot make a decision without the scores.
Placing deployment early means real users meet an unchecked change. Think about which step must come last because it only makes sense for a version that has already been approved.
Work backwards: the final step is the one that continues after launch. Before it comes the decision, before that the measuring, and at the very start the material that makes measuring possible.
questions.deep: Keep the evaluation dataset versioned and refresh it with failures found in production, so each release is tested against the mistakes of the last one. The same evaluators can then run continuously on sampled live traffic. Microsoft Learn: Evaluate Microsoft Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/observability/how-to/evaluate-agent

questions.prompt: Match each operational question to the evidence that most directly answers it.
rows: Did groundedness degrade for sampled production answers?
Which retrieval or tool span caused the latency increase?
Who approved the state-changing action and with which arguments?
options: Continuous evaluation results
Correlated distributed traces
Immutable approval and provenance record
Subscription quota allocation
answer: Continuous evaluation results
Correlated distributed traces
Immutable approval and provenance record
questions.explain: Evaluation scores describe response quality, traces locate latency within an interaction, and approval records establish accountability for consequential actions. Quota data cannot substitute for any of those records.
questions.teach: Different operational questions need different evidence. Quality questions are answered by evaluation scores, timing questions by traces that break an interaction into spans, and accountability questions by records of who approved what. Capacity and quota figures are about the platform, not about a particular answer.
hints: Read each question for its verb. One asks whether quality got worse, one asks where time was spent, and one asks who is responsible for an action and what exactly was done.

Match the evidence to what it can show. A score can say that quality moved but not why. A trace can show where time went but is not a judgement of quality. A permanent record of a decision shows accountability.

One of the options is a platform capacity figure. It describes how much throughput the subscription holds and says nothing about quality, timing or accountability, so it fits none of the three questions and stays unused.
questions.deep: Make approval records tamper-evident and tie them to the exact arguments of the approved action. Quota data is useful for capacity planning, but it never answers a question about one response or one decision. Microsoft Learn: Evaluate Microsoft Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/observability/how-to/evaluate-agent

questions.prompt: Which four data elements are most useful for diagnosing latency and cost regressions after an agent release? Choose four.
options: Input, output, and cached token counts by model call
Prompt, workflow, tool-schema, and deployment version identifiers
Correlated spans for model, retrieval, handoff, and tool operations
Per-span duration, status, retries, and error details
Aggregate model latency and total token cost for the release without retaining per-operation spans
Store raw prompts and final answers but omit workflow, tool-schema, index, and deployment versions
answer: Correlated spans for model, retrieval, handoff, and tool operations
Input, output, and cached token counts by model call
Per-span duration, status, retries, and error details
Prompt, workflow, tool-schema, and deployment version identifiers
questions.explain: Correlated spans for model, retrieval, handoff and tool operations, token counts by call, per-span duration with status and retries, and version identifiers for prompt, workflow, tool schema and deployment let engineers compare releases and isolate regressions. Aggregates alone, or prompts and answers without version metadata, cannot attribute cost or latency to a change.
questions.teach: When an agent release makes things slower or more expensive, you need to know where. Time and cost are spread across model calls, retrieval, handoffs and tools, so you need per-operation data, not totals. You also need to know which prompt, workflow, tool schema and deployment versions were live, otherwise you cannot tie a change to a release.
hints: A regression is a difference between two releases. Ask what you must record so that you can compare the old and the new at the level of single operations.
Totals for the whole release can show that cost rose but cannot say which call grew. Raw prompts and answers without version information cannot tell you which release produced them.
The four useful data sets combine structure (how the operations fit together), volume (tokens), behaviour (duration, status and retries) and identity (versions of what ran).
questions.deep: Cached tokens are usually billed differently from uncached ones, so record them separately when you analyse cost. Retries inside a span are a common hidden source of both latency and spend. Microsoft Learn: Foundry agent tracing, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/observability/how-to/trace-agent-setup

questions.prompt: An agent's final message sounds correct, but production incidents show malformed tool arguments. What should the evaluation emphasize?
options: Only fluency of the final response
Only retrieval recall, even when no retrieval tool is involved
Tool input accuracy and task-adherence evidence from the agent trajectory
Only model token count, because malformed arguments always use more tokens
answer: Tool input accuracy and task-adherence evidence from the agent trajectory
questions.explain: Agent evaluation should inspect the process as well as the final answer. Tool-input accuracy checks whether required parameters, types, formats, and values are appropriate, while task adherence checks behavioral alignment.
questions.teach: A fluent final message does not prove the agent did the right things on the way. Agents act through tool calls, and a tool call can have wrong or malformed arguments while the closing summary still reads well. Agent evaluation therefore inspects the trajectory: whether the right tool was chosen, whether its inputs were correct, and whether the behaviour stayed aligned with the task.
hints: The symptom is a good-looking final message together with malformed tool arguments in production. The evaluation has to look where the failure is, which is before the final message.
Metrics that only grade the prose, or that count tokens, cannot see whether a parameter had the right type or value. Retrieval metrics are irrelevant when no retrieval tool is involved.
Choose the option that evaluates the inputs given to tools and whether the agent's actions matched what it was asked to do.
questions.deep: Evaluate at three levels: the single tool call, the whole trajectory, and the final answer. Malformed arguments are often best caught by strict schemas and validation in the tool layer, with evaluators measuring how often the model gets them wrong. Microsoft Learn: Evaluate Microsoft Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/observability/how-to/evaluate-agent

questions.prompt: Which function-tool definition is most likely to produce reliable calls?
options: A clear schema that declares properties but omits required fields and allows undeclared arguments
A constrained schema whose values are checked only in the browser before being sent to the backend
A descriptive tool name with one unconstrained string argument containing all requested work
A descriptive name, a clear purpose, a constrained JSON schema, required fields, and server-side argument validation
answer: A descriptive name, a clear purpose, a constrained JSON schema, required fields, and server-side argument validation
questions.explain: Clear semantics and a constrained schema help the model form valid calls. The application must still validate and authorize arguments before execution.
questions.teach: A function tool is described to the model by a name, a description and a JSON schema of its arguments. The model never runs your code: it only proposes a call that matches that description. The clearer and tighter the description, the more reliably the model proposes valid calls, and your code must still check every argument before acting on it.
hints: Think of the definition as the only instruction manual the model ever sees. A good manual says what the tool is for, exactly which inputs it takes, and which inputs are mandatory.
Weak definitions leave the model guessing: one catch-all text argument, or properties that exist but may be left out or extended freely. Each gap is a place where bad calls get through.
Also decide where validation happens. A check that runs only in the browser can be bypassed, so the strong option includes a check on the server side that executes the call.
questions.deep: Strict mode on a function tool makes the model's arguments conform to your schema, which removes parsing surprises but does not replace authorization checks. Keep tools small and single-purpose; a vague multi-purpose tool is harder for the model to call correctly. Microsoft Learn: Foundry Agent Service runtime components, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/runtime-components

questions.prompt: Which three practices are appropriate when adding a remote MCP server to a Foundry agent? Choose three.
options: Review or require approval for sensitive MCP tool calls
Use an approved project connection but give the agent access to every MCP tool under a subscription-level owner identity
Apply least privilege and validate tool arguments before side effects
Require approval for the first call to each MCP tool, then treat that tool as trusted for every later user and argument
Configure the MCP endpoint and its authentication through an approved project connection
answer: Configure the MCP endpoint and its authentication through an approved project connection
Review or require approval for sensitive MCP tool calls
Apply least privilege and validate tool arguments before side effects
questions.explain: MCP extends an agent with remote tools, so the connection, authentication, approvals, and execution boundary must be governed. Tool discovery does not replace authorization, validation, or secret management.
questions.teach: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an agent use tools hosted on a remote server. The server is outside your control, so you govern the connection: where the endpoint and credentials are configured, which calls need human approval, and how arguments are checked before anything with side effects happens. Discovering a tool does not authorize its use.
hints: A remote MCP server extends what the agent can do, so treat each option as a question about trust. Who configures the connection, who approves sensitive calls, and what limits the damage if a call is wrong?
Be careful with options that look like approvals but quietly grant too much: a broad owner-level identity, or a one-time approval that makes a tool trusted forever for every user and every input.
The correct practices cover three areas: a managed place for the endpoint and its authentication, human review for sensitive calls, and least privilege with argument validation before side effects.
questions.deep: Approval should apply per call and show the actual arguments, as in the mcp_approval_request flow, rather than being granted once per tool. Treat tool output from a remote server as untrusted input too, since it can carry injected instructions. Microsoft Learn: MCP tools for Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/tools/model-context-protocol

questions.prompt: A valid OpenAPI 3.1 document fails when registered as a Foundry agent tool because none of its operations can be selected. What should you verify first?
options: Each callable operation defines a unique supported operationId
The servers array contains the production URL even though callable operations don't define operationId
Each callable operation defines a unique operationRef while operationId is omitted
Each callable operation has a unique tag and summary but shares the same operationId
answer: Each callable operation defines a unique supported operationId
questions.explain: Foundry OpenAPI tools need each callable operation to define a unique supported operationId, which gives it a usable tool identity. A different construct such as operationRef, a missing identifier, or duplicates shared across operations leave the tools indistinguishable.
questions.teach: A Foundry OpenAPI tool turns each callable operation in an OpenAPI document into a function the agent can pick. To pick one, the agent needs a stable name for it, and that name comes from a field on each operation. If the field is missing or repeated, the operations cannot be told apart, even though the document is otherwise valid.
hints: The document passes OpenAPI validation but no operation can be selected. So the structure is fine and what is missing is something the tool layer needs in order to name each operation.
Ask what makes one operation different from another when the agent chooses between them. Look for the field that gives each operation its own identity, and whether it must be present and not shared.
Do not be distracted by fields about servers or by cross-reference constructs. Tags and summaries help readers, but they do not give an operation the identifier that tool registration relies on.
questions.deep: Choose operationIds that read like function names and stay stable between releases, since the model sees them. Keep schemas bounded and descriptions specific so two similar operations are not confused. Microsoft Learn: OpenAPI tools for Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/tools/openapi

questions.prompt: An agent tool creates shipping labels. A network timeout can occur after the backend creates a label but before the agent receives the response. Which design best prevents duplicates?
options: Query for an existing label before each retry, then issue an unkeyed create request when none is returned
Generate a stable idempotency key for the intended action and have the backend return the existing result on retry
Generate a new idempotency key for each retry so every HTTP request can be traced separately
Ask the model whether the first call probably succeeded and retry only when its confidence is low
answer: Generate a stable idempotency key for the intended action and have the backend return the existing result on retry
questions.explain: An idempotency key identifies one intended side effect across retries. The backend can record the completed operation and safely return the same label instead of creating another one after an ambiguous timeout.
questions.teach: A timeout is ambiguous: the request may have succeeded on the server even though the client never heard back. Retrying a create operation blindly can therefore create a duplicate. An idempotency key makes a retry safe. The caller sends the same unique key for the same intended action, and the server records the result and returns it again instead of repeating the work.
hints: Focus on the dangerous moment: the backend created the label but the response was lost. The agent now cannot tell whether to retry. What would make a retry harmless?
A key only helps if it identifies the intended action, not the individual network attempt. Ask whether the key stays the same or changes when the same action is retried.

Guessing success from a model's confidence, or checking and then sending an unkeyed request, still leaves a window for a duplicate. The reliable design puts the protection on the backend, keyed to the action.
questions.deep: Servers typically store the key with the response for a limited time and return the stored response when the same key reappears. Generate the key when the user's intent is formed, not when the HTTP request is built, so retries share it. Microsoft Learn: OpenAPI tools for Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/tools/openapi

questions.prompt: An OpenAPI tool exposes two operations with the same operationId and overlapping descriptions. What should be corrected first?
options: Remove authentication so the model can retry either operation
Convert every request property to an unconstrained string
Make each operationId unique and keep each schema and description specific
Give every operation the same shorter description
answer: Make each operationId unique and keep each schema and description specific
questions.explain: The agent uses operation metadata to select and call tools. Unique operation IDs plus precise descriptions and bounded schemas reduce ambiguity; removing authentication or constraints makes the integration less safe.
questions.teach: An agent chooses which tool operation to call by reading the operation names and descriptions. If two operations share an identifier or have overlapping descriptions, the choice becomes ambiguous and calls may go to the wrong place. Each operation needs its own identity, a specific description and a schema with sensible limits.
hints: The problem as stated is ambiguity: two operations that cannot be told apart. Think about what you would change first so that the model can tell them apart.
Changing both descriptions to be identical makes the ambiguity worse, not better. Removing authentication or loosening the schema makes the integration less safe without helping selection.
The fix gives each operation a distinct identifier and keeps every description and schema specific to what that operation does.
questions.deep: Write descriptions for the model, not for humans: say when to use the operation and when not to. Keep parameters typed and bounded so that choosing the right operation is also what makes the call valid. Microsoft Learn: OpenAPI tools for Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/tools/openapi

questions.prompt: Which two changes make an OpenAPI tool safer and easier for an agent to call correctly? Choose two.
options: Allow undeclared request properties so the model can improvise
Use unique operation IDs with precise operation descriptions
Put reusable API secrets in operation descriptions
Use bounded request schemas with required fields and appropriate authentication
answer: Use unique operation IDs with precise operation descriptions
Use bounded request schemas with required fields and appropriate authentication
questions.explain: Unique, descriptive operations and bounded authenticated schemas reduce ambiguity and constrain accepted actions. Undeclared arguments and secrets in descriptions expand the attack surface and weaken validation.
questions.teach: An OpenAPI tool is a contract between the agent and your API. A good contract is easy for the model to follow and hard to misuse: operations are named distinctly and described precisely, request bodies declare their fields with required ones marked, undeclared properties are not accepted, and authentication is handled by configuration rather than by the model.
hints: Evaluate each option as a change to a contract. Ask whether it narrows what the agent can send and makes the right call easier to choose, or whether it opens the door to improvisation.
Anything that lets the model add undeclared properties or that places credentials where the model can read them widens the attack surface. Those two options work against the goal.
The helpful changes come in a pair: one makes operations unambiguous to choose between, the other makes the inputs and access bounded.
questions.deep: Set additionalProperties to false on request schemas where the tooling supports it, and keep secrets in a project connection instead of the specification. The model should only ever see business parameters. Microsoft Learn: OpenAPI tools for Foundry agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/tools/openapi

questions.prompt: A diagnostic request must use the agent's configured file-search tool, but responses sometimes answer from model knowledge and omit citations. Which response setting directly addresses this behavior?
options: Raise temperature so the model explores more documents
Set max output tokens to the number of indexed files
Remove the vector store and place filenames in the system message
Set tool_choice to required for the response
answer: Set tool_choice to required for the response
questions.explain: For the documented file-search scenario, tool_choice='required' forces tool use for that response. It does not guarantee relevant evidence exists, so vector-store attachment and indexing must still be verified.
questions.teach: By default a model decides for itself whether to call an available tool, so it can answer from its own knowledge and skip retrieval. A response setting called tool_choice changes that: it can force the model to use a tool. Forcing the call does not create evidence, so the files still need to be indexed and attached for the call to return anything useful.
hints: The symptom is that the model sometimes answers from memory and gives no citations, even though the tool is configured. The tool is available but the model is not obliged to use it.
Ask which knob controls whether a tool must be used. Settings about randomness or output length do not change that decision, and removing the knowledge source makes things worse.
Look for a setting on the response itself that directs the model's choice about tools, rather than something about the prompt wording or the data.
questions.deep: Forcing a tool is a good test of whether retrieval works at all: if citations still fail, check that the vector store is attached to the agent and that indexing finished. Keep tool_choice flexible in normal chat, where a tool is not always needed. Microsoft Learn: File search tool for agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/tools/file-search

questions.prompt: A workflow drafts a payment request and a human must approve it. Where should the approval occur?
options: Before the payment tool, with the exact target and arguments shown to the reviewer
After the payment tool succeeds, so the reviewer sees the final transaction ID
Once when the agent version is created, covering all future payments
Inside the model's hidden reasoning, with no separate approval event
answer: Before the payment tool, with the exact target and arguments shown to the reviewer
questions.explain: Approval must gate the consequential operation and cover the exact action and arguments that will execute. Post-action notification, hidden model reasoning, or blanket version approval cannot prevent an unwanted transaction.
questions.teach: Approval is only a control if it happens before the thing it protects. For a consequential action such as a payment, the reviewer must decide before the tool runs and must see the concrete target and arguments that will be used. Notifying someone afterwards is an audit trail, not an approval.
hints: Ask what the approval is supposed to prevent. If the goal is to stop an unwanted payment, think about where in the sequence a no can still change the outcome.

A decision made after the money has moved, or made once for all future payments, cannot judge the specific request in front of the reviewer. A decision hidden inside the model leaves no separate event to point to.
The strong design pauses at the gate, shows the reviewer exactly what will be executed, and only then lets the tool run.
questions.deep: Bind the approval to the exact arguments, so a changed amount invalidates it. Persist the approval event with the reviewer, time and arguments, because that record is what an auditor will ask for. This was a preview feature when the source bank was checked, so confirm its current status on Microsoft Learn before relying on it. Microsoft Learn: Foundry workflows (preview), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/workflow

questions.prompt: Users upload supported manuals and expect an agent to answer from their contents with citations. The files are not part of an existing enterprise search index. Which tool is the most direct fit?
options: A content filter configured as the agent's knowledge source
The file search tool backed by an attached vector store
Conversation memory, because it automatically indexes uploaded binary documents
A reflection loop that asks the model to recall the manual
answer: The file search tool backed by an attached vector store
questions.explain: File search uploads and indexes supported documents in a vector store that can be attached to the agent. Memory stores user-level learned information; they are not a substitute for document ingestion and retrieval.
questions.teach: Agents get knowledge in different ways. A file search tool takes documents you upload, splits and indexes them in a vector store, and lets the agent retrieve and cite passages from them. Memory stores facts learned about a user. Content filters protect against harm, and a reflection loop is just the model critiquing its own output; none of those ingest documents.
hints: The need is to answer from uploaded manuals and cite them, and the files are not in any existing search index. So something has to take the files in, index them and make them searchable for the agent.
Rule out options whose job is something else: remembering user facts, filtering harmful output, or asking the model to recall text it has never been given.
Choose the tool that is designed to ingest documents and retrieve passages from them, backed by an indexed store that the agent can reach.
questions.deep: File search suits user-provided or case-specific documents, while a governed Azure AI Search index suits shared enterprise content that needs filters and scheduled ingestion. Scope vector stores per user or case so one customer's files are never retrievable by another. Microsoft Learn: File search tool for agents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/tools/file-search

questions.prompt: A Foundry workflow saved a user response as a local variable named Var01. Which expression returns its uppercase value?
options: ToUpper(Conversation.Var01)
Upper(Var01.Value.Text)
Upper(Local.Var01)
Upper(System.Var01)
answer: Upper(Local.Var01)
questions.explain: Foundry workflow Power Fx expressions prefix local variables with Local., and Upper transforms a string to uppercase. System. is reserved for documented system variables rather than saved local values.
questions.teach: Foundry workflows use Power Fx expressions to compute values. An expression combines functions, which transform values, with references to variables. Variables are grouped into scopes, shown as a prefix in front of the name, so the workflow can tell values it saved itself from values supplied by the platform.
hints: Break the expression into two parts: the function that changes the text, and the reference that points at the saved value. Check each part separately in the options.

For the reference part, think about who created the value. It was saved by the workflow during this run, so it belongs to the scope for values the workflow defines, not the scope reserved for values the platform provides.
For the function part, compare how the options spell the case-changing function and whether the extra suffixes after the variable name look like real syntax or like invented decoration.
questions.deep: Power Fx scopes in workflows separate system-supplied values from locally set ones, so a name collision cannot overwrite a platform value. Workflows are a preview capability, so re-check the expression reference when the feature updates. Microsoft Learn: Foundry workflows (preview), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/workflow

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the most suitable workflow pattern.
rows: Research output must always flow to a writer and then to a compliance reviewer
Specialists dynamically hand off a support issue based on context
A user must approve a proposed financial transaction
options: Sequential
Human in the loop
Group chat
answer: Sequential
Group chat
Human in the loop
questions.explain: Sequential is a fixed pipeline, group chat supports dynamic expert handoff, and human-in-the-loop pauses for input or approval.
questions.teach: A workflow is a defined way for agents and steps to cooperate. In a sequential pattern the steps always run in one fixed order and each passes its output on. In a group-chat pattern several specialists take part in a shared conversation and control moves between them as the context demands. A human-in-the-loop step pauses the flow so that a person can approve or provide input before it continues.
hints: For each scenario, find the single word that decides the pattern. One says 'always flow' through named stages, one says the route depends on context, and one says a person must say yes.
A fixed pipeline of stages in a set order is the simplest pattern. Compare it with the scenario where the next owner is chosen on the fly depending on what the issue turns out to be.
The scenario that involves a financial transaction needing approval is not about ordering or handoff at all. It is about stopping for a person. Each option is used once.
questions.deep: Workflows are a preview feature at the time of the source, so confirm the current pattern names before relying on them. Choose the least dynamic pattern that meets the requirement, since fixed flows are easier to test and trace. Microsoft Learn: Foundry workflows, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/workflow

questions.prompt: A triage agent must dynamically transfer work among billing, technical, and compliance specialists until the issue is resolved. Which pattern is the best fit?
options: A handoff workflow in which the active specialist transfers control and cannot rejoin the discussion
A concurrent fan-out workflow that runs all specialists once and merges their independent answers
A fixed sequential workflow that invokes billing, technical, and compliance once in the same order
A group-chat workflow with explicit participant roles and termination conditions
answer: A group-chat workflow with explicit participant roles and termination conditions
questions.explain: Group chat supports context-driven transfer among specialists. Clear roles, routing rules, limits, and termination criteria keep the orchestration bounded and traceable.
questions.teach: Multi-agent patterns differ in who decides what happens next. A sequential workflow fixes the order in advance. A concurrent fan-out runs several agents at once and merges their results. A handoff passes control to another agent. A group chat lets several specialists see the discussion and take turns as the issue evolves, and it needs roles and a stopping rule so it does not run forever.
hints: The need is that work must move among three specialists dynamically, based on how the issue develops, and may return until it is resolved. The word 'until' tells you the number of steps is not known in advance.

A fixed order that calls each specialist once, or a parallel run that merges independent answers, cannot react to what the previous specialist found. A handoff that never lets an agent come back also fails the 'until resolved' part.
The fitting pattern lets participants contribute repeatedly under clear roles, with explicit limits and a termination condition.
questions.deep: Always give a group chat a maximum number of turns and a clear completion condition, and trace each agent's identity so you can see who said what. Without limits, dynamic orchestration is the easiest pattern to run up cost. This was a preview feature when the source bank was checked, so confirm its current status on Microsoft Learn before relying on it. Microsoft Learn: Foundry workflows, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/workflow

questions.prompt: Which design is a safe use of model reflection for a generated report?
options: Generate a draft, evaluate it against explicit criteria, revise once or twice, and stop at a fixed limit
Give the critic publication tools so it can approve and publish any draft that passes self-critique
Continue drafting and critiquing until the critic assigns its own output a perfect score
Run one critic pass without explicit criteria, then accept every revision the creator produces
answer: Generate a draft, evaluate it against explicit criteria, revise once or twice, and stop at a fixed limit
questions.explain: A bounded draft-critique-revise loop can improve output while controlling cost and runaway behavior. Use explicit evaluation criteria and a deterministic stopping rule.
questions.teach: Reflection means asking a model to critique and improve its own draft. It can raise quality, but a loop that never stops can run up cost, and a critic that is allowed to act can overstep. A safe design uses explicit criteria for the critique, a small fixed number of revision rounds, and no authority to publish or approve.
hints: Judge each design on two points: does it improve quality in a controlled way, and does it keep the loop from running away or the critic from taking actions it should not?
A loop that runs until a model gives itself a perfect score has no reliable end, because the same model both writes and grades. A critic with no stated criteria gives vague feedback.
Give the critic no tools that can publish or approve. The safe option states what to check, limits the number of rounds, and stops at a fixed point.
questions.deep: Stop on a deterministic rule such as a maximum number of rounds or a score threshold from an independent evaluator, not on the generating model's own opinion. Keep publication and approval outside the reflection loop. This was a preview feature when the source bank was checked, so confirm its current status on Microsoft Learn before relying on it. Microsoft Learn: Foundry workflows, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/workflow

questions.prompt: A request must always pass through extraction, validation, and then summary, with each node consuming the previous node's saved output. Which workflow pattern is the clearest fit?
options: Group chat with unrestricted dynamic handoff
Sequential workflow
A shared memory store used as an execution engine
Independent parallel agents with no aggregation node
answer: Sequential workflow
questions.explain: A sequential workflow explicitly preserves the required processing order and passes outputs between nodes. Dynamic group chat or uncoordinated parallel work would not guarantee extraction before validation and summary.
questions.teach: When steps depend on each other and must happen in a fixed order, you want a pattern that states the order explicitly: each node runs after the previous one and receives its saved output. More dynamic patterns trade that predictability for flexibility, which is unwanted when the order is a hard requirement.
hints: Look for the words that fix the order: always, then, and each step using the previous step's saved output. Those words describe a pipeline.
A pattern in which agents choose who speaks next cannot guarantee that extraction happens before validation. A set of independent parallel agents with no step to combine them has no ordering at all.
A shared store is a place to keep data, not an engine that decides what runs when. Choose the pattern whose whole purpose is running ordered steps.
questions.deep: Sequential flows are the easiest to test, because each node has a known input and output. Save intermediate results so a failure in the third step can be replayed without repeating the first two. This was a preview feature when the source bank was checked, so confirm its current status on Microsoft Learn before relying on it. Microsoft Learn: Foundry workflows (preview), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/workflow

questions.prompt: A triage agent can delegate to billing or technical specialists. Which design makes the handoff most testable?
options: Give all agents identical broad instructions and let them compete to answer
Store routing decisions only in the final natural-language response
Define specialist responsibilities, handoff criteria, and structured context passed at transfer
Share one unrestricted tool credential and omit agent identities from traces
answer: Define specialist responsibilities, handoff criteria, and structured context passed at transfer
questions.explain: Explicit roles, routing criteria, and structured transfer context make delegation observable and evaluable. Identical roles and hidden routing decisions create ambiguous ownership and make failures difficult to reproduce.
questions.teach: In a multi-agent design, delegation should be explicit enough to test. Each agent has a defined responsibility, there are stated criteria for when control moves, and the context handed over is structured, so you can check afterwards whether the right agent was chosen and received what it needed. Identical, overlapping agents or hidden routing make failures hard to reproduce.
hints: The key word is testable. A design is testable when you can say in advance who should handle a case and why, and then check that this is what happened.
Designs where agents are interchangeable and compete, or where routing choices are buried in free text at the end, give you nothing definite to assert on.
Look for the option that writes down responsibilities, criteria for transfer, and a structured package of context that moves with the transfer.
questions.deep: Log the handoff decision and the reason as structured fields in the trace, and include a labelled set of tricky triage cases in your evaluation. Giving each agent its own identity and narrowly scoped tools also limits the damage of a wrong handoff. Microsoft Learn: Foundry Agent Service runtime components, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/runtime-components

questions.prompt: A backend calls the same prompt agent for many customers. Each customer may keep durable preferences, but no preference can be visible to another customer. Which memory-tool scope should be configured?
options: A scope based only on the Foundry project resource ID
A single static scope equal to the agent version name
The literal scope {{$conversationId}} with no user identity header
The per-user scope {{$userId}}, with the backend sending the appropriate memory user identity
answer: The per-user scope {{$userId}}, with the backend sending the appropriate memory user identity
questions.explain: The documented {{$userId}} scope resolves an end-user identity from the x-memory-user-id header or the caller's Entra identity. A static agent or project scope would intentionally share memory across users.
questions.teach: Agent memory stores durable facts, such as a customer's preferences, across conversations. Each memory is saved under a scope, and anyone who can use that scope can recall what is in it. If the scope is shared, one customer's memory can surface for another, so the scope must be derived from the end user's identity.
hints: The requirement is isolation: a preference saved for one customer must never appear for another. The scope is the key that decides who sees which memory.
Ask what each candidate scope varies with. A scope tied to the agent version, the project or even a single conversation does not vary by customer in the way required.
Look for the scope that resolves to the individual end user, together with a way for the backend to say which user is calling.
questions.deep: The end-user identity is supplied by the caller, either through a memory user header or the caller's Entra identity, so make sure your backend sets it correctly for every request. A missing or constant identity silently turns per-user memory into shared memory. Microsoft Learn: Foundry Agent Service memory, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/memory-usage?view=foundry

questions.prompt: An assistant must remember an order number during one support conversation, but policy forbids retaining it after that conversation ends. What should the design use?
options: Conversation state associated with that support session
A file-search vector store containing every conversation transcript
A shared memory store with a permanent static scope
A system message containing the latest order number for every user
answer: Conversation state associated with that support session
questions.explain: Conversation state preserves context within the active interaction without turning transient identifiers into durable cross-session memory. File search and a shared system message would create inappropriate persistence or disclosure.
questions.teach: There are two kinds of remembering. Conversation state holds what has happened during one interaction, so the assistant can follow along, and it goes away with that session. Durable memory persists facts across sessions, which is exactly what you do not want for an item that policy says must not be kept. Choosing the right layer is a privacy decision as well as a design one.
hints: Separate how long the information must live from how widely it can be seen. The order number is needed only while the conversation is open and must not outlive it.
Options that keep information permanently, in a shared store, a searchable collection of transcripts, or in text shared across users, all break the rule that it must disappear.

Pick the layer that is tied to the active interaction and has no life beyond it, so the identifier disappears together with the conversation instead of being stored where later sessions could read it.
questions.deep: Use durable memory only for information users would reasonably expect the assistant to keep, and give them ways to see and delete it. Transient identifiers such as order numbers belong in the conversation, not in a long-lived store. Microsoft Learn: Foundry Agent Service memory, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/memory-usage?view=foundry

questions.prompt: Which two practices are recommended when an agent stores durable user memory? Choose two.
options: Use one shared static scope so recommendations improve across customers
Retain every interaction indefinitely so deletion cannot affect model quality
Map the memory scope to the end user and enforce per-user access controls
Expose appropriate memory inspection and deletion controls and minimize sensitive content
answer: Map the memory scope to the end user and enforce per-user access controls
Expose appropriate memory inspection and deletion controls and minimize sensitive content
questions.explain: Memory should be isolated by user, minimized, protected, and governed with retention and deletion controls. A shared scope or indefinite retention creates avoidable privacy and cross-user disclosure risks.
questions.teach: Durable user memory is personal data stored on someone's behalf. It should be isolated per user, minimized so that only useful information is kept, protected with access controls, and governed with ways to inspect and delete it. Sharing a scope or keeping data forever might improve convenience but creates privacy and disclosure risk.
hints: Treat the memory store as a place that holds personal information. Ask for each option whether it protects the person or exposes them.

Reject the option that merges everyone's memories into one place so the assistant learns across customers, and reject the option that keeps everything indefinitely because deleting might change behaviour.
The two good practices are about boundaries between users and about control: who can see each memory, and what the person can do about what is stored.
questions.deep: Plan for deletion requests from the start, since removing a user's memories must be possible on demand. Avoid storing sensitive content in memory at all unless the scenario demands it, and keep retention periods short. Microsoft Learn: Foundry Agent Service memory, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/memory-usage?view=foundry

questions.prompt: Which three practices most directly improve the grounding of a RAG answer? Choose three.
options: Tell the model to answer from supplied evidence and abstain when evidence is insufficient
Use the largest possible fixed chunks without overlap so fewer records are placed in the search index
Always retrieve only the single highest-scoring chunk, regardless of score distribution or evidence coverage
Use chunking and overlap that preserve meaningful context
Retrieve relevant passages and include stable source metadata
answer: Use chunking and overlap that preserve meaningful context
Retrieve relevant passages and include stable source metadata
Tell the model to answer from supplied evidence and abstain when evidence is insufficient
questions.explain: Meaningful chunking with overlap, retrieving relevant passages together with stable source metadata, and telling the model to answer from supplied evidence and abstain when it is insufficient most directly improve grounding. Always taking one top chunk, or using the largest fixed chunks with no overlap, throws away evidence the answer may need.
questions.teach: Grounding means the model's answer is tied to evidence you supplied. Three habits improve it. Chunk documents so each piece keeps enough surrounding context to make sense. Retrieve relevant passages and carry stable source metadata with them so the answer can cite its sources. Instruct the model to rely on the supplied evidence and to say so when the evidence is not enough.
hints: Walk through the pipeline from documents to answer and ask where grounding can be lost: when documents are cut up, when passages are selected, and when the model writes the answer.

Be careful with options that take a shortcut at one stage: always keeping only the top hit regardless of how strong it is, or making chunks as large as possible without overlap to save storage. Both reduce the quality of the evidence.
The three helpful practices correspond to the three stages: meaningful chunks, relevant passages with source information, and an instruction that discourages guessing.
questions.deep: Ground-truth checks need passages that actually contain the answer, so measure retrieval quality separately from generation quality. An explicit abstain instruction is cheap and reduces confident but unsupported answers. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search vector search overview, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-overview

questions.prompt: Which three practices make citations in a RAG response reproducible? Choose three.
options: Keep stable document and chunk identifiers with source URLs and version metadata
Validate that returned citation identifiers were present in the retrieved context
Pass retrieved source identifiers alongside the text supplied to the model
Keep the document URL but omit chunk identifiers and effective-version metadata from retrieval results
Prompt the model to include plausible source URLs and accept them whenever the URL format is valid
answer: Keep stable document and chunk identifiers with source URLs and version metadata
Pass retrieved source identifiers alongside the text supplied to the model
Validate that returned citation identifiers were present in the retrieved context
questions.explain: Stable source metadata must survive indexing, retrieval, and generation. Validating cited identifiers against the actual retrieved set prevents fabricated links and makes the answer traceable to a specific evidence version.
questions.teach: A citation is only useful if someone can follow it back to the exact evidence. That requires stable identifiers and version information kept through indexing and retrieval, source identifiers handed to the model together with the text, and a check afterwards that every citation in the answer really came from the retrieved context. Models can invent plausible-looking references if nothing checks them.
hints: Ask what would let a reviewer reproduce a citation next month: the same document, the same chunk and the same version of it. The metadata has to survive every stage.
Prompting the model to include plausible-looking links, or keeping only a document URL while dropping chunk and version information, leaves citations that cannot be reproduced or verified.
The right practices cover keeping identifiers stable, passing them along with the passages, and checking the model's output against what was actually retrieved.
questions.deep: Post-generation validation is cheap: reject or repair any citation ID that is not in the retrieved set. Store the effective version of each chunk so a citation still resolves after the source document changes. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search vector search overview, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-overview

questions.prompt: An inspection app must answer, 'Is the pressure gauge above the red threshold?' based only on a photo. Which design is best?
options: Use a custom object detector to locate the gauge, then assume any detected gauge is above threshold
Send the image and question to a multimodal model and require an answer grounded in visible evidence
Run OCR on the gauge labels and infer the needle position from the recognized threshold text
Compare an image embedding with labeled high- and low-pressure examples and return the nearest label
answer: Send the image and question to a multimodal model and require an answer grounded in visible evidence
questions.explain: A multimodal model can reason over the image and question together. Requiring visible evidence reduces unsupported conclusions.
questions.teach: Visual question answering means answering a natural-language question about an image. A multimodal chat model accepts the image and the question together and reasons over both. Narrower tools, such as OCR for reading text or an object detector for locating things, answer narrower questions, and none of them can judge a needle position or a threshold on its own.
hints: Look at what the question needs from the photo: a judgement about where a needle sits relative to a mark. That is a visual relationship, not just text or a label.
Tools that read printed labels, find objects or compare against labelled examples each solve part of a different problem. Ask whether any of them can actually see where the needle is.
Choose the approach that lets one model look at the image and the question together, and that asks it to base the answer on what is visible.
questions.deep: Ask the model to quote the visible evidence and to say when the image is not clear enough, then route those cases to a human or a re-capture. Without an uncertainty path, a multimodal model may answer with false confidence. Microsoft Learn: Vision-enabled chat models in Microsoft Foundry, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/gpt-with-vision

questions.prompt: A team is creating a new Azure image-generation deployment after March 2026. Which model family should it evaluate?
options: A DALL-E 3 deployment created after its new-deployment retirement date
An image-embedding model used to retrieve the nearest existing asset
A supported GPT-image series model
A vision-capable chat model that accepts images but doesn't expose an image-generation operation
answer: A supported GPT-image series model
questions.explain: Microsoft documents DALL-E 3 as retired on March 4, 2026. New Azure image-generation solutions should use a supported GPT-image series model selected for the required quality, editing, latency, and cost characteristics.
questions.teach: Models have lifecycles: they are released, supported for a time, and retired. When a model is retired, new deployments of it can no longer be created, and Microsoft publishes the retirement dates. For image generation on Azure, you should check the current model list rather than reusing a model name from older tutorials.
hints: The stem sets a date: a deployment created after March 2026. That tells you to think about which models are still available to deploy then, not which was popular earlier.
Two options cannot generate images in the first place: one is a chat model that merely accepts images as input, and one produces embeddings for retrieval. Rule them out on capability alone.
Between the remaining two, ask which one is described as a supported, current family and which one is described as being created after its retirement date.
questions.deep: Model retirements are announced on the Foundry Models and image generation pages, and they affect existing deployments as well as new ones. Build model names into configuration, not code, so a migration is a deployment change. Microsoft Learn: Azure OpenAI image generation models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/dall-e

questions.prompt: A supported GPT-image workflow must generate a product cutout with a transparent background. Which output configuration is appropriate?
options: Leave the background on auto and request JPEG output
Request an opaque background with PNG output
Request a transparent background with JPEG output
Request a transparent background and use PNG output
answer: Request a transparent background and use PNG output
questions.explain: Transparency requires an image format that supports an alpha channel, such as PNG, together with the supported transparent-background option. JPEG output cannot preserve transparency.
questions.teach: A transparent background needs two things to line up. The model has to be asked to produce transparency, and the file format has to be able to store it. PNG has an alpha channel that holds transparency, while JPEG does not, so a transparent cutout can only be delivered as PNG.
hints: Treat this as a pair of settings that must agree: one about the content of the image, and one about the container the image is saved in.
Think about what an image file needs in order to describe pixels that show nothing behind them. One of the two common formats in the options has no way to record that.
Reject any option that either asks for a solid background or lets the background be chosen automatically. The task needs transparency to be explicitly requested.
questions.deep: Check the model's documentation for which parameters it supports, since transparency options differ across image models. Always test with a viewer that shows a checkerboard behind transparent pixels. Microsoft Learn: Azure OpenAI image generation models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/dall-e

questions.prompt: Which three capabilities are supported by current GPT-image series workflows in Azure? Choose three.
options: Accept text and image inputs for supported generation or editing scenarios
Request a transparent background while using JPEG output
Return every generated image as a hosted URL instead of inline base64 data
Return generated image data as base64 output
Use a mask and prompt to constrain an edit to selected areas
answer: Accept text and image inputs for supported generation or editing scenarios
Use a mask and prompt to constrain an edit to selected areas
Return generated image data as base64 output
questions.explain: Current GPT-image models accept text and image input, support editing with a mask and a prompt, and return generated images as base64 data. They do not return every image as a hosted URL, and transparency cannot be combined with JPEG output.
questions.teach: GPT-image series models work with both text and images. They can generate new images, edit existing ones with a prompt, and constrain edits to a region with a mask. In Azure, the generated image comes back as encoded image data in the response. Format and transparency options interact: transparency needs a format that supports it.
hints: Treat each option as a claim about what the models support, and test it against what you know about generation and editing workflows.
Two options contradict how these workflows are described in the documentation: one says every image is returned as a hosted link, and one pairs transparency with a format that cannot store it.
The three supported capabilities cover the input side (what you can send), the control side (how to limit an edit), and the output side (what comes back).
questions.deep: Because images come back as base64 rather than a link, your application must decode and store them itself. Check input_fidelity and quality settings, which affect how closely edits follow the source. Microsoft Learn: Azure OpenAI image generation models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/dall-e

questions.prompt: A user asks whether a photographed control panel has a damaged connector, but the connector is outside the frame. How should a grounded multimodal assistant respond?
options: Explain that the image does not show the connector and request a suitable photograph
Infer the connector's condition from the visible warning light
State that the connector is damaged because that is the safer assumption
Generate a likely connector image and analyze the generated pixels
answer: Explain that the image does not show the connector and request a suitable photograph
questions.explain: A visually grounded answer must distinguish observed evidence from missing information. Requesting another image is appropriate when the required region is absent; inference or generated imagery cannot establish the real connector's state.
questions.teach: A grounded visual answer separates what can be seen from what is merely assumed. If the evidence needed to answer is not in the picture, a trustworthy assistant says so and asks for better evidence. Inventing, inferring from something nearby, or generating a picture to analyse produces a confident answer that is not about the real object.
hints: The key detail is that the part in question is outside the frame. Ask what a careful human inspector would say if given only this photo.

Options that infer the answer from something that is visible, or default to a cautious guess, both turn missing evidence into a claim. Generating an image to analyse studies a made-up object, not the real one.
The response that serves the user is the one that is honest about the gap and tells them how to fix it.
questions.deep: Put the uncertainty path in the system prompt and in your evaluation set: include photos where the answer is not visible and check that the assistant declines to guess. For safety-relevant inspections, send unresolved cases to a person. Microsoft Learn: Use vision-enabled chat models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/gpt-with-vision

questions.prompt: An image-generation response contains b64_json rather than a public URL. What should the application do to persist the generated image?
options: Send the value to Translator before storing it
Base64-decode the value to bytes and write those bytes using the intended image format
Store the encoded string directly in a .png file without decoding
Treat b64_json as a Blob Storage URL and issue an HTTP GET
answer: Base64-decode the value to bytes and write those bytes using the intended image format
questions.explain: The b64_json field carries base64-encoded image bytes. The application must decode it before writing an image file; treating it as a URL or writing the text itself produces an invalid artifact.
questions.teach: Image-generation APIs can return either a link to the image or the image data itself. The b64_json field holds the image bytes encoded as base64 text, which is a way of writing binary data using only text characters. To get a usable image file, an application decodes that text back into bytes and writes the bytes out.
hints: Think about what the field contains. It is not an address you can fetch; it is the picture itself, written down as text so it can travel inside JSON.
A file saved with the encoded text inside it is a text file with an image extension, and no viewer will open it. Sending the value to a translation service has nothing to do with images.
The step you need turns the text representation back into the original binary content before it is written to disk in the right format.
questions.deep: In Python this is base64.b64decode on the field, then writing the bytes to a file opened in binary mode. Keep the file extension consistent with the output format you requested. Microsoft Learn: Azure OpenAI image generation, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/dall-e

questions.prompt: Which two instructions best support useful, evidence-grounded alt text? Choose two.
options: State uncertainty or omit details that cannot be verified from the image
Infer product claims that are likely true even when they are not visible
Describe information needed to understand the image's purpose and context
Always produce the longest possible description regardless of page context
answer: Describe information needed to understand the image's purpose and context
State uncertainty or omit details that cannot be verified from the image
questions.explain: Accessible descriptions should communicate relevant visible information and represent uncertainty honestly. Unsupported claims and mechanically long output can mislead users and obscure the image's actual purpose.
questions.teach: Good alt text tells someone who cannot see an image what they need to know in context. It describes information relevant to the page, and it does not guess. When a detail cannot be confirmed from the image, the right move is to say so or to leave it out. Longer is not better: length should follow purpose.
hints: Imagine a reader who depends on this text. What helps them is relevant information and honesty, not a long list of every pixel and not guesses about what is probably true.
Reject instructions that encourage inventing claims that are likely but not visible, and instructions that push for the longest possible output no matter where the image is used.
The two good instructions are about relevance to purpose and about how to treat details that cannot be verified.
questions.deep: Tell the model where the image appears and what the surrounding text already says, so it does not repeat it. Allow it to answer that the image is unreadable, and send those cases for review. Microsoft Learn: Use vision-enabled chat models, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/gpt-with-vision

questions.prompt: Partner images can contain unsafe imagery and printed instructions intended to manipulate the agent. Which two controls address these distinct risks? Choose two.
options: Increase image resolution so hidden instructions become trustworthy
Classify the image with the applicable content-safety controls
Run Prompt Shields or equivalent document-attack detection on untrusted grounding content
Let the vision model follow printed instructions before the system message
answer: Classify the image with the applicable content-safety controls
Run Prompt Shields or equivalent document-attack detection on untrusted grounding content
questions.explain: Content classification and indirect prompt-attack detection address different threat categories and should be layered. Better resolution does not establish trust, and untrusted text must never override system policy.
questions.teach: Partner images can be risky in two separate ways. The picture itself may contain unsafe content, which is a classification problem. The picture may also carry text, or be accompanied by documents, that tries to instruct the model, which is an attack-detection problem. Different detectors address each, and they are used together.
hints: Name the two risks in the stem: unsafe imagery, and printed instructions meant to manipulate the agent. They need different kinds of controls.
Options that try to solve trust by making the image clearer, or by letting the model obey whatever the picture says, do not address either risk and can make the second one worse.
Pair one control that classifies what the image shows with one that screens untrusted text for attempts to take control of the model.
questions.deep: Treat any text extracted from an external image as untrusted data, the same as a web page. Screening it with a document attack detector before it reaches the model, and keeping system instructions in a higher-priority role, are complementary defences. Microsoft Learn: Prompt Shields for documents, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-safety/quickstart-jailbreak

questions.prompt: Which three outputs can a generative text-analysis flow produce directly from customer feedback? Choose three.
options: Page-coordinate bounding polygons for every extracted phrase
Structured JSON whose properties and types conform to a supplied output schema
A concise feedback summary constrained by the application's review instructions
Named entities and topics extracted into the declared feedback-analysis structure
Word-level speaker timestamps for each feedback item
answer: Named entities and topics extracted into the declared feedback-analysis structure
A concise feedback summary constrained by the application's review instructions
Structured JSON whose properties and types conform to a supplied output schema
questions.explain: A generative text-analysis flow can extract entities and topics, summarize, and return structured JSON that follows a supplied schema. Word-level speaker timestamps come from speech recognition, and bounding polygons come from document layout analysis, so neither is produced from feedback text alone.
questions.teach: A generative text-analysis flow reads text and returns something derived from it: entities and topics, a summary, a classification, or a structured object with fixed fields. It cannot return information that was never in the text, such as audio timings or positions on a page, because those come from speech recognition or document layout analysis.
hints: Ask of each option: is this something you can compute from the words of customer feedback alone? If it needs audio or a page image, a text-analysis step cannot produce it.
Two options describe outputs that belong to other services entirely, one tied to spoken audio and one tied to the position of text on a scanned page.
The three outputs that fit are the ones a language model can derive straight from the text: pulling out items, shortening it, and returning it in a declared shape.
questions.deep: Combine a schema with validation so the extracted structure is dependable downstream. For classic tasks such as sentiment, key phrases or PII, the Azure Language service is the prebuilt alternative to prompting. Microsoft Learn: Azure Language in Foundry Tools, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/language-service/overview

questions.prompt: Legal reviewers need compliance summaries with fixed headings and citations to clauses. What is the best first implementation?
options: Fine-tune a model on prior summaries and accept free-form output without a schema or citation validation
Use a structured prompt and examples but rely on model memory instead of retrieving the governing clauses
Use a domain-specific prompt with examples, a structured schema, retrieved clauses, and an evaluation set
Use extractive summarization and add headings afterward without retrieving or preserving clause identifiers
answer: Use a domain-specific prompt with examples, a structured schema, retrieved clauses, and an evaluation set
questions.explain: Grounding, domain instructions, examples, and a schema target the required format. An evaluation set tests whether summaries and citations meet compliance needs.
questions.teach: When a use case needs a fixed format and traceable citations, you combine several techniques instead of relying on one. Retrieval supplies the governing text, a schema fixes the structure, instructions and examples shape the style, and an evaluation set checks whether the result meets the standard. Fine-tuning alone does not give citations, and model memory is not a source of truth.
hints: Write down what the reviewers need: fixed headings, citations to specific clauses, and trust that the content is right. Each need maps to a different technique.
Options that rely on the model's memory of the clauses, or that bolt headings on afterwards and lose clause identifiers, cannot deliver citations that point to the real source.
Look for the answer that brings the clauses into the prompt, fixes the output shape, includes examples, and gives you a way to measure the result.
questions.deep: Compliance output deserves automatic checks: confirm that every cited clause ID exists in the retrieved set and that required headings are present. Start with prompting and retrieval before considering fine-tuning.
