Microsoft Learn: Structured outputs with Azure OpenAI, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/structured-outputs

questions.prompt: A support application must locate personal identifiers in free text and produce a version suitable for downstream diagnostics with those entities obscured. Which capability should it use?
options: Semantic ranking with captions disabled
Translator transliteration with the target script set to Latin
Speech synthesis with word-boundary events
Azure Language PII detection and its redacted text output
answer: Azure Language PII detection and its redacted text output
questions.explain: Azure Language PII detection identifies supported personal-information categories and can return redacted text. Translation, synthesis, and semantic ranking do not provide entity-level PII recognition and redaction.
questions.teach: Personally identifiable information (PII) detection is a feature of Azure Language. It finds entities such as names, phone numbers and account numbers in free text, classifies them by category, and can return a version of the text with those entities masked. That masked copy is what you pass on to systems that should not see the originals.
hints: The task has two parts: locate personal identifiers in unstructured text, and produce a copy in which they are obscured. Ask which service category does entity recognition on text.
Options about translating scripts, producing speech with timing events, or ranking search results do not recognise entities in text, so they cannot find identifiers.
Choose the capability that specialises in recognising sensitive entities and that can hand back a redacted version.
questions.deep: PII detection returns categories, offsets and confidence scores, and the redacted text is a convenience, not a guarantee, so test it on your own data. Run it before text enters logs, traces or analytics. Microsoft Learn: PII detection in Azure Language, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/language-service/personally-identifiable-information/overview

questions.prompt: Which two practices best reduce accidental disclosure when processing support transcripts for diagnostics? Choose two.
options: Retain entity category and position information only where the diagnostic workflow actually requires it
Assume redaction is unnecessary when the transcript was produced by Speech rather than typed by a user
Write the original transcript to every trace before running detection
Run PII detection before placing transcript content in ordinary diagnostic logs
answer: Run PII detection before placing transcript content in ordinary diagnostic logs
Retain entity category and position information only where the diagnostic workflow actually requires it
questions.explain: PII controls should occur before broad diagnostic propagation, and retained sensitive metadata should be minimized to the workflow's needs. Speech-derived text can contain the same personal information as typed text.
questions.teach: Privacy controls work best early. Once raw personal data has been written to logs or traces it spreads to every system that stores them. Detect and redact before the text reaches ordinary diagnostics, and keep only the metadata you really need. Text that came from speech recognition is just as sensitive as typed text.
hints: Think about where personal data could escape: into logs and traces that many people and tools can read. The best control is applied before that happens, not after.
Two options argue for convenience or for assuming a source is safe: writing the original everywhere first, and assuming spoken input needs no redaction. Neither reduces the chance of disclosure.
The right practices place detection ahead of the logging step and limit retained metadata to what the diagnostic workflow requires.
questions.deep: Keep a correlation ID so diagnostics can still join redacted text to latency and error data. Apply least retention to anything that remains, including entity categories and positions. Microsoft Learn: PII detection in Azure Language, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/language-service/personally-identifiable-information/overview

questions.prompt: Match each requirement to the Azure Speech capability.
rows: Turn a recorded call into text
Read an agent answer in a natural voice
Convert live spoken French into English text
Control pauses, pronunciation, rate, and pitch
options: SSML
Speech translation
Speech to text
Text to speech
answer: Speech to text
Text to speech
Speech translation
SSML
questions.explain: Recognition transcribes, synthesis produces audio, speech translation changes language during recognition, and SSML controls synthesized speech characteristics.
questions.teach: Azure Speech groups several capabilities. Speech to text turns audio into text. Text to speech turns text into audio. Speech translation recognises speech and returns text in another language while the person is still talking. SSML, the Speech Synthesis Markup Language, is not a separate engine: it is markup you add to text to control how it is spoken.
hints: For each requirement, ask what goes in and what comes out. Audio in and text out, text in and audio out, audio in one language and text out in another, or a fine-grained control over how speech sounds.
Two rows are close cousins: one turns a recording into words, the other changes the language along the way. The difference is whether the output language is the same as the spoken language.
The row about pauses, pronunciation, rate and pitch is not a service that converts anything. It is the markup you use to shape synthesized output. Each option is used once.
questions.deep: Speech translation uses the Speech SDK and can return interim and final results, with optional synthesized audio in the target language. SSML can set voice, style, prosody, phonemes and breaks, and different voices support different SSML features. Microsoft Learn: Azure Speech documentation, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/speech-service/

questions.prompt: A voice agent must pronounce a product name correctly and pause before reading a warning. What should you supply to text to speech?
options: SSML with pronunciation and break controls
Set speaking rate and pitch in the SDK request but leave the product pronunciation and pause unspecified
Supply a plain-text utterance plus a pronunciation lexicon but no markup for the required pause
Train a custom voice for the product name and insert punctuation where the warning pause should occur
answer: SSML with pronunciation and break controls
questions.explain: SSML is designed to control pronunciation, pauses, speaking rate, pitch, volume, voice, and other speech-synthesis properties.
questions.teach: Text to speech reads out whatever text it is given, using default pronunciation and pacing. When you need to control details, such as how a brand name sounds or where to pause before a warning, you send SSML, which wraps text in tags that describe pronunciation, breaks, rate, pitch and more.
hints: List the two things the agent needs: a particular pronunciation of one word, and a pause at a particular point. Ask what mechanism can express both inside the text that is sent for synthesis.

A setting for overall rate or pitch applies to the whole utterance and cannot fix one word or insert one pause. Punctuation is only a weak hint to the voice, and training a custom voice is far heavier than the need.
Choose the option that lets you annotate specific words and specific positions in the utterance with markup, rather than adjusting a setting that applies to the whole sentence in the same way.
questions.deep: SSML supports phonemes for exact pronunciation, a lexicon file for reusable pronunciations, and break elements for timed pauses. Prefer SSML over training a custom voice unless the voice itself must be new. Microsoft Learn: Azure Speech documentation, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/speech-service/

questions.prompt: Match each audio workload to the most suitable Speech capability.
rows: Live microphone input with interim results
One stored recording that needs a synchronous transcript quickly
Thousands of recordings already held in Blob Storage
Recurring domain vocabulary needs model adaptation and measured accuracy gains
options: Custom Speech
Real-time transcription
Batch transcription
Fast transcription
answer: Real-time transcription
Fast transcription
Batch transcription
Custom Speech
questions.explain: Real-time transcription handles streams, fast transcription synchronously handles a single stored file, batch transcription processes large stored collections asynchronously, and Custom Speech adapts recognition to domain data.
questions.teach: Speech to text comes in several modes. Real-time transcription handles live audio and returns interim results as people talk. Fast transcription processes a single stored file synchronously and quickly. Batch transcription processes many stored recordings asynchronously. Custom Speech adapts recognition to your vocabulary with your own data and lets you measure the improvement.
hints: Sort the four workloads by two questions: is the audio live or stored, and is it one file or many? Then look separately for the one row about adapting to vocabulary.

Live microphone input with partial results needs a mode designed for streams. A single stored file that must return quickly is the synchronous case, and thousands of files in storage is the volume case.
The last row is not about how audio arrives but about accuracy for domain words, which is solved by training with your data and measuring. Each option is used once.
questions.deep: Batch transcription is submitted by reference to files in storage and returns results asynchronously, with diarization and word-level timestamps as options. Custom Speech models also have lifecycles and expiry, so plan to retrain. Microsoft Learn: Speech to text REST API, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/speech-service/rest-speech-to-text

questions.prompt: A live demo repeatedly misrecognizes twelve new product names. The team needs a quick runtime improvement without training a custom model. What should it use?
options: Use pronunciation assessment to score each recognized product name and substitute low-scoring results
A phrase list supplied to the speech recognizer
Create a custom neural voice that pronounces the product names correctly during text-to-speech output
Train a custom Speech model on labeled recordings of the twelve names before the live demo
answer: A phrase list supplied to the speech recognizer
questions.explain: A phrase list can bias speech recognition toward a small set of expected words or names at runtime. It is faster to apply than training a custom model, though broader persistent accuracy needs may justify Custom Speech.
questions.teach: A phrase list is a lightweight way to improve recognition at runtime. You give the recogniser a list of words or names you expect to hear, and it leans toward them without any model training. It suits a small, known set of terms, whereas a large or permanent vocabulary gap is a case for Custom Speech.
hints: Weigh the constraints: only twelve names, a live demo, and a need for a quick improvement without training anything. The tool should be applicable at the moment of recognition.

Training with labelled recordings is the heavyweight route for a bigger problem. Pronunciation assessment scores how a person speaks, and a custom neural voice is about how a system talks, not about what it hears.
Look for the option that simply tells the recogniser which words to expect during this session, so the short list of names is favoured without any training run before the live demo.
questions.deep: A phrase list applies to the current recognizer session and is cheap to change between runs. If misrecognition persists across many terms or accents, move to Custom Speech with real audio and text data. Microsoft Learn: Improve recognition with phrase lists, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/speech-service/improve-accuracy-phrase-list

questions.prompt: Which three text-to-speech behaviors can SSML directly control? Choose three.
options: The audio container, codec, and sample rate selected for the synthesized output file
Pronunciation through SSML phonemes or a referenced pronunciation lexicon
Pauses, emphasis, and sentence delivery through SSML prosody elements
Voice selection together with speaking rate, pitch, volume, and other prosody controls
The Azure region and deployment capacity assigned to a custom voice endpoint
answer: Pronunciation through SSML phonemes or a referenced pronunciation lexicon
Pauses, emphasis, and sentence delivery through SSML prosody elements
Voice selection together with speaking rate, pitch, volume, and other prosody controls
questions.explain: SSML controls pronunciation (phonemes or a referenced lexicon), pauses and emphasis through prosody, and the voice with its rate, pitch and volume. The audio container, codec and sample rate are set in the synthesis output configuration, and region or capacity belong to the Azure resource, not to SSML.
questions.teach: SSML describes how synthesized speech should sound: how words are pronounced (phonemes or a lexicon), where to pause and what to emphasise, and which voice to use with settings like rate, pitch and volume. It does not decide how the audio file is packaged or where a service runs; those are set elsewhere in the request or in Azure.
hints: Ask of each option whether it is about how the speech sounds or about how it is delivered or hosted. SSML works at the level of sound and delivery of the voice.
The container, codec and sample rate are properties of the output audio file. The Azure region and capacity are properties of the resource. Neither is written in the markup.
The three correct options are the three families of sound control: saying words correctly, shaping rhythm and emphasis, and choosing the voice along with its prosody.
questions.deep: Not every voice supports every SSML element, so test the voice you ship. Use a lexicon for pronunciations shared across many utterances and inline phonemes for one-off fixes. Microsoft Learn: Azure Speech documentation, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/speech-service/

questions.prompt: A Speech REST request returns 401 after a team copies a resource key from West Europe but sends the request to an East US regional endpoint. What should it do first?
options: Use the global Speech endpoint with the regional key but omit the resource region from configuration
Regenerate the West Europe key and continue sending it to the East US regional endpoint
Use the endpoint or region that belongs to the Speech resource associated with that key
Acquire a token for an East US Speech resource while continuing to identify the West Europe resource in the request
answer: Use the endpoint or region that belongs to the Speech resource associated with that key
questions.explain: Speech credentials and regional endpoints must refer to the same resource context. A 401 is an authentication problem, so the team should verify the matching key, resource endpoint, region, and authorization header before changing audio settings.
questions.teach: A Speech resource key is valid only for the resource it belongs to, and each resource lives in a region with its own regional endpoint. A 401 Unauthorized response means the service could not authenticate the request, and a mismatch between the key and the endpoint or region is a frequent cause.
hints: Read the facts: the key came from one region's resource and the request went to a different region's endpoint. A credential and the place it is presented have to belong together.
Regenerating a key changes the secret but leaves the mismatch, and mixing a token for one resource with identification of another keeps two different resources in play.
The first fix is to make the key, the resource and the endpoint or region all refer to the same Speech resource.
questions.deep: When a 401 appears, verify in order: the key or token, the region named in the endpoint, and the resource's custom domain if it has one. Fix authentication before touching audio settings. Microsoft Learn: Speech to text REST API for short audio, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/speech-service/rest-speech-to-text-short

questions.prompt: A nightly job must transcribe 8,000 long recordings already stored in Blob Storage. Interactive partial results are not required. Which capability should the solution use?
options: Continuous real-time recognition, with one long-running recognizer allocated to every Blob recording
Fast transcription, submitting each complete long recording through a synchronous request
Conversation transcription, with a live session kept open while each stored file is played into it
Azure Speech batch transcription for asynchronous processing of the Blob-hosted recordings
answer: Azure Speech batch transcription for asynchronous processing of the Blob-hosted recordings
questions.explain: Batch transcription is an asynchronous service for large volumes of prerecorded audio in storage. Real-time recognition is intended for live or interactive streams and would add unnecessary orchestration for a nightly historical workload.
questions.teach: Batch transcription is the asynchronous way to transcribe large amounts of recorded audio held in storage. You submit a job that points at the files, and you collect results later. Other modes, such as real-time recognition or synchronous fast transcription, assume live or one-file-at-a-time work and would force you to build a lot of coordination yourself.
hints: Note the workload: eight thousand long recordings, already in Blob Storage, processed overnight, with no need for live partial results.
Modes designed for live conversation need an open session per recording, and a synchronous mode returns one answer at a time. Orchestrating thousands of those is extra work for no benefit.
Choose the mode designed for large volumes of stored audio where you submit work and fetch results afterwards.
questions.deep: Batch transcription reads files by URL, so the service has to be given access to the storage account, for example through a SAS URL. Results come back as JSON and can include diarization and timestamps. Microsoft Learn: Azure Speech batch transcription, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/speech-service/batch-transcription

questions.prompt: A Custom Speech model expires before the team updates its deployments. What behavior should operations expect?
options: The custom endpoint falls back to the newest base model for the same locale, while a batch request that names the expired model fails with a 4xx error
Both routes continue using the expired custom model indefinitely because it was previously deployed
Both custom endpoints and batch transcription silently use any model in any locale
The custom endpoint returns a 2xx response with no transcript, while batch transcription retrains the model automatically
answer: The custom endpoint falls back to the newest base model for the same locale, while a batch request that names the expired model fails with a 4xx error
questions.explain: The documented behaviors differ: a custom endpoint falls back to the newest base model for its locale, potentially reducing domain accuracy, while batch transcription requests that reference an expired model fail with a client error.
questions.teach: Custom Speech models have a lifecycle and eventually expire. What happens afterwards differs by route. A custom endpoint keeps working but quietly falls back to a base model, which can hurt accuracy on your domain vocabulary. A batch request that names the expired model is rejected with a client error. Operations need a runbook that covers both behaviours.
hints: The answer has two halves because there are two ways of using the model. One is a live endpoint; the other is a one-off job that names a model explicitly.
Think about what each route can do when the thing it points at is gone. A live endpoint cannot simply go dark, whereas a request that names a specific missing model can be refused as a bad request.
Be sceptical of options that say a model retrains itself, lives forever, or produces server errors. The documented behaviour is a fallback on one route and a client error on the other.
questions.deep: Silent fallback is the dangerous case, because requests still succeed while recognition of your product names gets worse. Monitor word error rate or key-term hit rate and track expiry dates so you retrain before expiration. Microsoft Learn: Custom Speech model lifecycle, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/speech-service/how-to-custom-speech-model-and-endpoint-lifecycle

questions.prompt: A document pipeline must translate millions of already-extracted text segments. No audio is involved. Which capability is the most direct fit?
options: Convert the segments to synthetic speech and use Speech Translation on the generated audio
Azure Translator Text in Foundry Tools, called directly for each already-extracted text segment
Send every segment to a general language model with a translation instruction and no terminology controls
Create temporary documents from the segments and submit each file to Document Translation
answer: Azure Translator Text in Foundry Tools, called directly for each already-extracted text segment
questions.explain: Azure Translator is the direct prebuilt service for text translation. Speech translation is appropriate when the input is audio or a live spoken stream.
questions.teach: Azure Translator has separate capabilities for different inputs. Text translation takes strings and returns translated strings. Document translation works on whole files and keeps their layout. Speech translation is for audio. If the input is already plain text, calling text translation directly is the shortest path.
hints: Identify the input: millions of already-extracted text segments, with no audio involved. The best service is the one whose input is exactly that.
Wrapping text into files to use a file-based service, or turning text into speech so that a speech service can hear it, adds steps that serve no purpose.
A general-purpose language model can translate, but a dedicated translation service is the more direct and controllable fit for this volume.
questions.deep: Text translation accepts several strings in one request, which suits high volumes, so batch your segments rather than sending them one by one. When files must keep their layout, switch to document translation. Microsoft Learn: Azure Translator documentation, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/translator/

questions.prompt: A single customer message alternates between French and German phrases. Translator returns incomplete English output. What is the documented mitigation?
options: Submit the entire message without a source language and increase max tokens
Use document OCR because OCR automatically resolves mixed-language sentences
Split the input into single-language segments and translate each with its intended source language
Transliterate the message before every translation request
answer: Split the input into single-language segments and translate each with its intended source language
questions.explain: Translator does not reliably support sentences containing mixed-language text. Segmenting the content into single-language units and specifying the intended source language avoids asking one request to interpret conflicting language context.
questions.teach: Translation services expect text in one language at a time. When a single message alternates between languages, automatic detection and translation can return incomplete output. The documented workaround is to cut the message into single-language pieces and tell the service the intended source language for each.
hints: The failure is tied to the input: one message mixes two languages. Ask what you can change about the input before sending it, rather than about the model or the output.
Increasing token limits, transliterating the text, or running OCR on it does not remove the mix of languages from a single request.
The fix breaks the problem into smaller parts that each have one language and then tells the service which language each part is.
questions.deep: Segment boundaries can follow sentences or phrases, and you can use language detection per segment when the source language is unknown. Reassemble the translated parts in order afterwards. Microsoft Learn: Azure Translator known issues, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/translator/reference/known-issues

questions.prompt: Arrange the processing stages for a message that contains several language-homogeneous segments.
tray: Translate each segment with its intended source and target language
Determine or validate the source language for each segment
Reassemble the outputs in order and apply any required human quality review
Separate the message into language-homogeneous segments
answer: Separate the message into language-homogeneous segments
Determine or validate the source language for each segment
Translate each segment with its intended source and target language
Reassemble the outputs in order and apply any required human quality review
questions.explain: The mitigation begins by isolating single-language inputs, then associating each with the proper source language. Translation occurs per segment before ordered reconstruction and any review required by the scenario.
questions.teach: Translating mixed-language text is a small pipeline. You first separate the message into parts that each contain one language, then work out which language each part is in, then translate every part with that source and the target language, and finally put the results back in order, adding review when the use case needs it.
hints: Think about what each step needs as input. You cannot choose a source language for a segment that has not been separated yet, and you cannot translate before the language is known.
Reassembly is the last step because it needs the translated pieces. Review comes after the text has been put back together.
Start with the step that fixes the cause of the problem: the mixture of languages in one string. Everything else depends on it.
questions.deep: If you can detect languages automatically per segment, keep the detected language and its confidence in your logs. Low-confidence segments are good candidates for the human review step. Microsoft Learn: Azure Translator known issues, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/translator/reference/known-issues

questions.prompt: Arrange the integrated RAG steps in the correct end-to-end order.
tray: Extract content and split it into useful chunks
Store text, metadata, and vectors in the search index
Retrieve passages and add them to the generation context
Generate embeddings for the chunks
Vectorize the user's query and run the search
Connect an indexer or ingestion process to the content source
answer: Connect an indexer or ingestion process to the content source
Extract content and split it into useful chunks
Generate embeddings for the chunks
Store text, metadata, and vectors in the search index
Vectorize the user's query and run the search
Retrieve passages and add them to the generation context
questions.explain: Ingestion connects to content, extracts and chunks it, embeds chunks, and stores them. Query time vectorizes the query, retrieves relevant passages, and grounds generation with those passages.
questions.teach: A RAG system has two phases. At ingestion time, content is connected, extracted, split into chunks, turned into embeddings and stored with its metadata in an index. At query time, the user's question is turned into a vector, the index returns the best passages, and those passages are placed in the prompt so the model can answer from them.
hints: Separate the six steps into those that happen before any user asks a question and those that happen because a user asked. The first group comes first and builds the index.
Inside ingestion, follow the data: you must reach the content before you can extract it, split it before you can embed the pieces, and have vectors before you can store them.
Inside the query phase, the question must be converted before the search can run, and results must be retrieved before they can be used to ground the generation.
questions.deep: The embedding model used for chunks and for queries must be the same, otherwise vectors do not live in the same space. Many teams add hybrid search and reranking between retrieval and generation to improve relevance. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search vector search overview, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-overview

questions.prompt: Match each search stage to its ranking method or score.
rows: Full-text keyword ranking
Approximate nearest-neighbor vector ranking
Fusion of keyword and vector result lists
Secondary semantic reranking
options: BM25
@search.rerankerScore
HNSW similarity
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
answer: BM25
HNSW similarity
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
@search.rerankerScore
questions.explain: BM25 ranks text, HNSW supports vector nearest-neighbor search, RRF combines parallel result lists, and semantic ranking reports a separate reranker score.
questions.teach: Azure AI Search ranks results in layers. Keyword search ranks documents by a text-relevance formula. Vector search finds the nearest neighbours in embedding space using an approximate algorithm. Hybrid search merges the keyword list and the vector list into one using a fusion method. Semantic ranking is a separate reranking pass that produces its own score.
hints: Treat the right-hand options as names for scoring methods and the left-hand rows as stages. The stages run roughly in order from first retrieval to final reranking.
The first two rows are two parallel retrieval styles, one based on words and one based on vectors. The third row exists because the two lists need to be combined, so it needs a fusion method.
The last row refers to a second pass that reorders the top results and reports a separate relevance score under its own field name. Each option is used once.
questions.deep: Fused scores from RRF depend on rank position rather than raw score, so they are not comparable with BM25 or similarity scores. The semantic reranker score is reported separately and only applies to the top results it re-scores. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search hybrid ranking, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/hybrid-search-ranking

questions.prompt: Arrange the Azure AI Search enrichment pipeline components in their logical order.
tray: Define the supported data source
Apply the skillset to enrich or transform content
Configure the indexer to read source documents
Map or project enriched output into the target index
answer: Define the supported data source
Configure the indexer to read source documents
Apply the skillset to enrich or transform content
Map or project enriched output into the target index
questions.explain: The data source identifies input, the indexer reads it, the skillset enriches the content, and mappings or projections write the results to searchable index structures.
questions.teach: An Azure AI Search enrichment pipeline is built from four pieces. A data source says where the content lives, an indexer reads it, a skillset applies enrichment steps such as OCR or splitting, and mappings or projections decide which enriched values land in which index fields.
hints: Think of the pieces as a chain in which each one needs the one before it. Something has to tell the service where the content is before anything can read it.
The component that enriches content works on documents that have already been read, so it cannot be the first or the second step.
The final step is about where the results are written. It needs the enriched output to exist first, so it cannot come before the step that produces that output.
questions.deep: Field mappings run on the source document before enrichment, while output field mappings and index projections run after it. Mixing up the two is a common reason enriched fields never appear in the index. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search vector search overview, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-overview

questions.prompt: An enrichment pipeline splits each manual into many chunks. Every chunk must be a searchable document that repeats the parent manual ID and revision. What should the skillset configure?
options: Use only indexer fieldMappings to copy the parent document into one target search document
Use outputFieldMappings for enriched values but omit the index projection that creates child documents
Store one search document per manual with all chunks in a collection field and no repeated parent fields
Index projections that map enriched child chunks and parent fields into the target index
answer: Index projections that map enriched child chunks and parent fields into the target index
questions.explain: Index projections support one-to-many indexing patterns such as document chunking. They map each child chunk plus repeated parent metadata into the search index and can omit separate parent documents when appropriate.
questions.teach: Chunking turns one source document into many search documents, which is a one-to-many relationship. Plain field mappings copy values into a single index document, so they cannot create the child documents. Index projections are the feature that lets a skillset write one index document per enriched chunk and copy parent fields onto each of them.
hints: The target shape is many searchable documents per manual, each carrying the parent's ID and revision. The question is which feature can create more than one index document from one source document.

Mapping features that copy values into a single document keep a one-to-one relationship. Storing all chunks in a single collection field keeps everything inside one document and does not repeat the parent fields on each chunk.
Choose the skillset-level feature that is built for one-to-many indexing patterns such as chunking, where one source document becomes many search documents that each repeat the parent's fields.
questions.deep: A parent key field on each chunk lets you filter or group results by manual and delete stale chunks when a document changes. Plan the projection mode so that re-indexing does not leave orphaned child documents. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search index projections, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-how-to-define-index-projections

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant vector index must exclude every document from other tenants before nearest-neighbor scoring. Which vector-filter mode should the query use?
options: preFilter, so the tenant predicate runs before vector candidate scoring
No service filter; include the tenant rule in the grounding prompt after retrieval
postFilter, which applies the tenant predicate after vector candidates have been selected
strictPostFilter, which filters only the final global top-k vector results
answer: preFilter, so the tenant predicate runs before vector candidate scoring
questions.explain: Pre-filtering applies the filter while the vector query is executed, so ineligible tenant documents are excluded from the candidate search. Prompt instructions and semantic captions are not data-isolation controls.
questions.teach: A vector query can apply a filter in different ways. With a pre-filter, the filter narrows the set of documents before nearest-neighbour search, so results come only from permitted documents. A post-filter runs after the nearest neighbours are chosen, which can leave fewer results than requested. Neither is replaced by instructions in a prompt.
hints: The rule is about data isolation: documents from other tenants must never take part in the nearest-neighbour step. That is a statement about when the filter is applied.

Filters that run after the top results have been selected may throw away some or all of them, and they have already let other tenants' documents compete. A prompt instruction runs after retrieval and cannot undo that.
Look for the mode in which the tenant condition is applied while the candidate set is formed, before scoring.
questions.deep: A pre-filter is also better for recall with selective filters, because the search is restricted to eligible vectors instead of discarding results afterwards. Always enforce tenant filters on the server side, never in client code or prompts. Microsoft Learn: Vector query filters in Azure AI Search, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-filters

questions.prompt: An existing Azure AI Search index has a tenantId field that was created with filterable set to false. The field must now support authorization filters. What should the team do?
options: Create an index alias for the existing index and set the alias itself to filterable
Add a new filterable field and repopulate it, or rebuild the index with the corrected schema
Keep the field nonfilterable and enforce the tenant predicate in a semantic configuration
Change filterable to true in the existing index definition and rerun the indexer without rebuilding documents
answer: Add a new filterable field and repopulate it, or rebuild the index with the corrected schema
questions.explain: Azure AI Search does not let an existing field be changed to filterable in place. The supported choices are a new field populated with the desired attribute or an index rebuild; prompt instructions are not an authorization filter.
questions.teach: In Azure AI Search, the attributes of a field, such as filterable, sortable and facetable, are fixed in the index schema, because they decide how the field is physically stored. Changing them on an existing field is not supported in place. The practical routes are to add a new field with the right attributes and populate it, or to rebuild the index.
hints: The field already exists with filtering switched off, and now you need to filter on it. Ask whether the service can flip that switch for an existing field.

An alias only points at an index, so it has no field attributes to change. A semantic configuration is about ranking, not about authorization. Rerunning an indexer does not alter the stored structure.
Think about the standard approach when a schema attribute is wrong: build the correct structure alongside and fill it with the data.
questions.deep: Treat the schema as part of the data model and plan attributes up front: filterable, sortable and facetable fields cost storage and indexing work. Use index aliases afterwards to switch applications to the rebuilt index without code changes. Microsoft Learn: Text query filters in Azure AI Search, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-filters

questions.prompt: An Azure AI Search indexer must split long documents into chunks and generate an Azure OpenAI vector for every chunk. Which skill pair directly implements those two stages?
options: Custom Web API skill followed by Semantic ranking
Document Extraction skill followed by Key Phrase Extraction skill
Text Split skill followed by Azure OpenAI Embedding skill
OCR skill followed by Sentiment skill
answer: Text Split skill followed by Azure OpenAI Embedding skill
questions.explain: The Text Split skill performs chunking and the Azure OpenAI Embedding skill converts each chunk into a vector during indexing. Semantic ranking is a query-time ranking capability rather than an embedding skill.
questions.teach: Integrated vectorization adds two stages to indexing. A splitting skill cuts long text into chunks of a manageable size, and an embedding skill calls an embedding model to turn each chunk into a vector. The stages run inside the skillset, so the index receives chunks with vectors ready for search.
hints: Name the two jobs in the stem: cutting long documents into pieces, and producing a vector for each piece. You need one skill for each job.
Skills for reading text from images, scoring sentiment, extracting key phrases or calling your own web service do not chunk or embed. Ranking at query time is not an indexing skill at all.
Choose the pair that performs those two jobs in that order, with the second one relying on an embedding model you have deployed.
questions.deep: Choose chunk size and overlap to match your embedding model's input limits and your retrieval needs. Pair the skill with a vectorizer on the index so queries are embedded with the same model. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search integrated vectorization, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-integrated-vectorization

questions.prompt: A Blob indexer must expose embedded document images at /document/normalized_images/* for downstream image skills. What should be configured?
options: Add a semantic configuration named normalized_images
Store base64 images in the search document key field
Set parsingMode to text and disable every image action
Set imageAction to generateNormalizedImages in the applicable extraction or indexer configuration
answer: Set imageAction to generateNormalizedImages in the applicable extraction or indexer configuration
questions.explain: A non-none imageAction such as generateNormalizedImages produces the normalized image collection used by downstream enrichment. Query ranking and key-field choices do not extract embedded images.
questions.teach: To run OCR or other image skills on pictures embedded in documents, the indexer must first extract those pictures. A setting on the indexer or on the Document Extraction skill, imageAction, controls this. When it is not set to none, the service produces a collection of normalized images that downstream skills can read.
hints: The goal is to make embedded images available at a particular path in the enrichment tree. Something upstream must produce them; later skills only consume what exists.
Settings that disable image handling, add ranking configuration, or put image data in the key field do not produce an image collection.
Look for the extraction-time setting that asks the service to generate the normalized images, because later skills such as OCR can only consume pictures that an earlier step has already produced.
questions.deep: Normalized images are resized and rotated into a consistent form so that OCR and vision skills behave predictably. Extracting images increases indexing time and cost, so enable it only for content that needs it. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search Document Extraction skill, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/cognitive-search-skill-document-extraction

questions.prompt: Which two configurations are required for consistent integrated vectorization at indexing and query time? Choose two.
options: Use a skillset that chunks content and generates vectors during indexing
Configure a vectorizer on the index that matches the embedding model used for indexed content
Remove the vector field and store vectors only in the semantic configuration
Use unrelated embedding models for indexing and query-time vectorization to increase diversity
answer: Use a skillset that chunks content and generates vectors during indexing
Configure a vectorizer on the index that matches the embedding model used for indexed content
questions.explain: The indexer-driven skillset creates chunk vectors, and the index vectorizer converts text queries with the same embedding model. Mismatched vector spaces cannot be compared meaningfully, and semantic configuration does not store vectors.
questions.teach: Integrated vectorization has an indexing side and a query side. During indexing, a skillset chunks content and creates a vector for each chunk. During querying, a vectorizer defined on the index converts the user's text into a vector. Both sides must use the same embedding model, otherwise their vectors are not comparable.
hints: Think about the two moments when text has to become a vector: when documents are indexed, and when a user searches. Each moment needs its own configured component.
Vectors from different embedding models live in different spaces, so mixing models for variety makes the comparison meaningless.
Semantic configuration is for ranking and does not store vectors. The correct pair is one component per moment, tied to the same embedding model.
questions.deep: If you change the embedding model, re-vectorize the whole index, because old and new vectors are not interchangeable. Keep model name and dimensions in configuration so the skillset and vectorizer cannot drift apart. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search integrated vectorization, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-integrated-vectorization

questions.prompt: Arrange the indexing path from source content to searchable chunk vectors.
tray: Index projections or field mappings write chunks and vectors to the target index
The chunking skill divides extracted content into bounded units
The indexer retrieves content from the configured data source
The embedding skill creates a vector for each chunk
answer: The indexer retrieves content from the configured data source
The chunking skill divides extracted content into bounded units
The embedding skill creates a vector for each chunk
Index projections or field mappings write chunks and vectors to the target index
questions.explain: The indexer drives data retrieval, enrichment first creates chunks and then their vectors, and mappings or projections persist the enriched outputs. Query-time vectorization occurs later when users search.
questions.teach: Indexing with integrated vectorization is a pipeline run by the indexer. The indexer reads content from the data source, a chunking skill divides the text into bounded pieces, an embedding skill creates a vector for each piece, and projections or mappings write the chunks and vectors into the index. Query-time vectorization happens later and is a separate path.
hints: The stem asks for the indexing path, from source content to searchable chunk vectors. Follow the content as it changes form: stored document, then pieces, then vectors, then index entries.
A vector can only be created for a piece that already exists, so the step that makes pieces comes before the step that makes vectors.
The last step is the one that persists results to the index, since there is nothing to persist until the previous steps have run.
questions.deep: The indexer is also what gives you incremental behaviour: only changed documents are reprocessed on later runs, which is why resetting the indexer matters after you add a new skill. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search integrated vectorization, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-integrated-vectorization

questions.prompt: A pipeline must extract invoice fields from scanned PDFs while preserving tables and layout context. Which three capabilities are required? Choose three.
options: Language detection and key-phrase extraction before sending the original page text to the model
Semantic reranking of previously extracted invoice text without OCR or layout-aware field extraction
Layout and table analysis that preserves rows, columns, and spatial relationships
Optical character recognition that recovers text from every scanned invoice page
Field extraction that maps invoice values and line items into a declared schema
answer: Optical character recognition that recovers text from every scanned invoice page
Layout and table analysis that preserves rows, columns, and spatial relationships
Field extraction that maps invoice values and line items into a declared schema
questions.explain: OCR recovers text from scans, layout analysis preserves structural relationships, and field extraction maps evidence to the required invoice schema.
questions.teach: Pulling invoice fields out of scanned PDFs takes three capabilities in sequence. Optical character recognition (OCR) turns pixels into text. Layout and table analysis keeps the structure, so a number stays attached to its row and column. Field extraction maps the values into the schema you declare, such as supplier, total and line items.
hints: A scan is just an image, so the first thing you need is a way to turn it into text. That is the capability that makes all later steps possible.
Invoices hold tables of line items, so reading words in order is not enough. You also need something that preserves rows, columns and where things sit on the page.
The last piece turns the text and structure into the fields the business wants. Options about detecting the language of the text, or about reranking search results, belong to different pipelines.
questions.deep: Document Intelligence and Content Understanding both combine these steps, with prebuilt models for standard documents and custom analyzers or models for others. Pay attention to confidence scores per field, since scans of poor quality produce uncertain values. Microsoft Learn: Content Understanding analyzers, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-understanding/concepts/analyzer-reference

questions.prompt: Which three analyzer features directly support structured extraction with reviewer-verifiable evidence? Choose three.
options: Markdown or structured content output for downstream reasoning
Declare the field schema but disable detailed output and discard confidence and source locations
Use a layout-only analyzer without the custom business fields required by downstream automation
A fieldSchema that declares the values and structures to extract
Detailed output with confidence, text spans, bounding regions, or source metadata
answer: A fieldSchema that declares the values and structures to extract
Detailed output with confidence, text spans, bounding regions, or source metadata
Markdown or structured content output for downstream reasoning
questions.explain: The field schema defines the machine contract, detailed source and confidence information supports verification, and structured or Markdown content supports downstream workflows. Discarding provenance undermines grounded review.
questions.teach: A Content Understanding analyzer is a reusable definition of what to extract and in what form. The field schema declares the values and structures you want. Detailed output can attach confidence, text spans, bounding regions or media positions to each value so a reviewer can verify it. Markdown or structured content output provides a readable representation for downstream reasoning.
hints: The stem has two goals at once: structured extraction, and evidence a reviewer can verify. List what each goal needs from the analyzer's configuration.

For structure, you need a declaration of the values to extract. For verification, you need information about where each value came from and how sure the system is. A readable content form helps later steps.
Reject any option that removes evidence or the business fields, such as turning off detailed output or using only layout with no custom fields.
questions.deep: Confidence and source location let you build a review queue that shows only uncertain fields and links each one to the exact region in the original file. Without them, automation either trusts everything or reviews everything. Microsoft Learn: Content Understanding analyzers, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-understanding/concepts/analyzer-reference

questions.prompt: Arrange the main stages of a layout-aware Azure AI Search ingestion pipeline.
tray: Apply the Document Layout skill to extract structure and create semantic chunks
Read source documents through the data source and indexer
Use index projections to write child chunks and parent metadata to the index
Generate embeddings for the layout-aware chunks
answer: Read source documents through the data source and indexer
Apply the Document Layout skill to extract structure and create semantic chunks
Generate embeddings for the layout-aware chunks
Use index projections to write child chunks and parent metadata to the index
questions.explain: The indexer first reads source content, the Document Layout skill extracts structure and chunks it, embeddings are generated for those chunks, and index projections map the enriched child documents into the search index.
questions.teach: Layout-aware chunking keeps meaningful structure such as headings, tables and sections when splitting a document, so each chunk is a coherent unit rather than an arbitrary slice of text. In Azure AI Search, the Document Layout skill extracts that structure and produces semantic chunks, embeddings are created for them, and index projections write the chunks with parent information to the index.
hints: As in any ingestion path, content must be read before it can be processed. Identify the step whose only purpose is bringing the source documents into the pipeline.
Embeddings are created for pieces that already exist, so the step that makes layout-aware pieces must come before the step that makes vectors.
The step that writes child chunks with their parent's metadata into the index is last, because it stores what the earlier steps produced.
questions.deep: Keep a parent identifier on every chunk so citations can link back to the original document. Check the Learn page for the skill's region availability and billing requirements before you choose it. Microsoft Learn: Document Layout skill for semantic chunking, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-how-to-semantic-chunking

questions.prompt: A workload extracts vendor, invoice number, dates, totals, and line items from common business invoices. It needs the most direct supported starting point. Which tool should it use?
options: The Document Intelligence prebuilt invoice model
A custom Content Understanding analyzer with natural-language fields matching the standard invoice schema
A Document Intelligence custom neural model trained on labeled copies of the common invoice format
A Document Intelligence custom template model trained separately for every vendor layout
answer: The Document Intelligence prebuilt invoice model
questions.explain: Document Intelligence provides a prebuilt invoice model for standard invoice fields and line items, so it is the most direct starting point and needs no labelling or training. Custom neural or template models and a custom Content Understanding analyzer add work that standard invoices do not need.
questions.teach: Document Intelligence offers prebuilt models for common document types, including invoices, and custom models you train for your own formats. When the documents are standard, a prebuilt model needs no labelling or training and returns known fields such as vendor, dates, totals and line items.
hints: The documents are common business invoices and the stem asks for the most direct supported starting point. Ask which option requires the least preparation.

Training a custom model, in any style, means collecting and labelling examples. A newly configured natural-language analyzer is a flexible tool but is aimed at varied content, not at a standard that already has a specialised model.
Choose the option that is purpose-built for exactly this document type, because a specialised model for standard invoices needs the least preparation and returns the usual fields straight away.
questions.deep: Start with the prebuilt model, measure field accuracy on your own invoices, and only then consider custom models for the gaps. Content Understanding is the better fit when document types vary widely or other modalities are involved. Microsoft Learn: Choose a document-processing Foundry Tool, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-understanding/choosing-right-ai-tool

questions.prompt: An intake package can include free-form letters, photographs, recorded interviews, and highly varied PDFs. The team wants inferred fields described in natural language without first labeling training data. What should it configure?
options: A Document Intelligence custom neural model trained separately for letters, photographs, recordings, and PDFs
A custom Content Understanding analyzer with a field schema
A routing pipeline of prebuilt document models, OCR, and Speech with application-written rules for all inferred fields
A composed Document Intelligence model containing one labeled extraction model for every incoming modality
answer: A custom Content Understanding analyzer with a field schema
questions.explain: Content Understanding custom analyzers support documents, images, audio, and video and can infer schema-described fields from unstructured content without labeled training examples. A single structured-document prebuilt cannot cover the multimodal package.
questions.teach: Document Intelligence is strongest for document-centric extraction with prebuilt models or models trained on labelled examples. Content Understanding custom analyzers work across documents, images, audio and video, and can infer fields that you describe in natural language, without a labelled training set. The mix of media and the absence of labelled data decide between them.
hints: Collect the clues: several kinds of media in one package, highly varied layouts, fields to be inferred from descriptions, and no labelled training data.
Approaches that need labelled examples for each media type, or that combine several prebuilt models with hand-written rules, fail the 'no labelling' clue or the 'varied media' clue.
Choose the tool built for schema-described extraction across several media types, which lets you describe fields in plain words and avoids collecting labelled examples first.
questions.deep: A custom analyzer is defined once with a field schema and can be reused across files. For stable, standard forms where accuracy per field is critical, a Document Intelligence model remains a strong choice. Microsoft Learn: Choose a document-processing Foundry Tool, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-understanding/choosing-right-ai-tool

questions.prompt: A company has labeled examples of a structured application form across several visual variants and needs custom field extraction. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Train a Document Intelligence custom template model and require every visual variant to use identical field positions
Train a custom classifier to identify each visual variant, then use prebuilt layout without custom field extraction
Train a Document Intelligence custom neural model with buildMode set to neural
Create a composed model containing only prebuilt models and route by the application's form name
answer: Train a Document Intelligence custom neural model with buildMode set to neural
questions.explain: A Document Intelligence custom neural model is designed for custom extraction from labeled structured or semi-structured documents with layout variation. The training build mode is neural; unrelated media and ranking services do not train field extraction.
questions.teach: Document Intelligence custom models are trained on labelled examples. A template model assumes fields sit at consistent positions, so it suits fixed forms. A neural model learns from labelled examples and generalises across layout variation, so it suits structured or semi-structured documents that come in several visual variants. The build mode selects which kind is trained.
hints: Note the situation: labelled examples exist, the form has several visual variants, and custom field extraction is required. Each fact narrows the choice.
A model that requires identical field positions cannot cope with variants. Models built only from prebuilt components or classifiers do not learn your custom fields at all.
Choose the model type designed to learn from labelled examples across layout variation, and remember that the build mode is how you ask for it.
questions.deep: A classifier can still help when different forms arrive mixed together: classify first, then route each class to its own extraction model. Plan labelling effort per field, since quality tracks the variety in your training set. Microsoft Learn: Train a custom neural Document Intelligence model, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/document-intelligence/train/custom-neural?view=doc-intel-4.0.0

questions.prompt: Which three design choices make a custom Content Understanding result useful for automated processing and human verification? Choose three.
options: Return one free-form text field and let downstream code infer every business value without typed declarations
Retain confidence and source-grounding information such as spans, regions, or media intervals
Declare the fields but disable detailed output so confidence and source grounding aren't retained
Declare typed business fields and descriptions in the field schema
Enable the content and modality features needed for OCR, layout, tables, charts, audio, or video
answer: Declare typed business fields and descriptions in the field schema
Retain confidence and source-grounding information such as spans, regions, or media intervals
Enable the content and modality features needed for OCR, layout, tables, charts, audio, or video
questions.explain: A typed field schema supplies the machine contract, modality-appropriate extraction preserves useful content, and confidence plus grounding supports reviewer verification. Discarding evidence or auto-approving uncertain fields undermines reliable automation.
questions.teach: A custom Content Understanding result is useful when machines can consume it and people can check it. Typed fields with descriptions give the machine contract. Confidence and grounding, such as spans, regions or media intervals, let a reviewer verify a value. Turning on the modality features the content needs, such as OCR, layout, tables, audio or video, ensures the evidence is actually extracted.
hints: Ask what a downstream program needs and what a human reviewer needs. The program wants typed, named values. The reviewer wants to see how sure the system is and where each value came from.
A single free-form text field pushes all the structure onto downstream code, and disabling detailed output throws away the very information used for review.
The three good choices cover the contract, the evidence and the features that must be switched on to produce that evidence.
questions.deep: Use confidence thresholds to route low-confidence fields to a person and let high-confidence ones pass automatically. Keep the schema stable and versioned, since downstream code depends on its field names and types. Microsoft Learn: Content Understanding analyzers, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-understanding/concepts/analyzer-reference

questions.prompt: An intake package can contain free-form PDFs, photographs, audio, and video, and the output must follow one custom business schema. Which service is the better primary fit?
options: Azure AI Search semantic ranking without an ingestion pipeline
Translator document translation without an extraction schema
A fixed-layout Document Intelligence custom template model for every media type
Content Understanding with a schema-based multimodal analyzer
answer: Content Understanding with a schema-based multimodal analyzer
questions.explain: Content Understanding analyzers are designed for schema-based extraction across documents, images, audio, and video. Document Intelligence remains strong for supported document-centric and stable-layout workloads but is not a universal multimedia parser.
questions.teach: Content Understanding analyzers are designed for schema-based extraction from documents, images, audio and video in one approach. Document Intelligence remains strong where the work is document-centric or the layout is stable, but it does not read audio or video.
hints: The package mixes documents, photographs, audio and video, and the output has to follow one business schema. The tool must handle all those media types.
Fixed-layout models are built for forms with stable positions and cannot cover audio or video. A translation feature or a ranking feature does not extract fields into a schema.
Choose the service whose analyzers are described as covering all four media types with a custom schema.
questions.deep: A single analyzer per use case keeps the output contract consistent across media types. Test with representative samples of each modality, since extraction quality differs between a clean PDF and a noisy phone recording. Microsoft Learn: Content Understanding analyzer reference, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-understanding/concepts/analyzer-reference

questions.prompt: Match each downstream requirement to the most useful extraction output.
rows: Run OCR over images embedded in an indexed PDF
Send validated invoice values to a line-of-business API
Preserve headings and tables for grounded document reasoning
options: Structured JSON matching the business schema
Search service quota metrics
Layout-aware Markdown representation
normalized_images collection
answer: normalized_images collection
Structured JSON matching the business schema
Layout-aware Markdown representation
questions.explain: Normalized images feed visual enrichment, structured JSON supports deterministic business integration, and layout-aware Markdown preserves useful document organization for reasoning. Quota metrics are operational rather than extracted content.
questions.teach: Extraction pipelines produce different outputs for different jobs. Normalized images are the pictures pulled out of a document so that visual enrichment such as OCR can run on them. Structured JSON that follows a schema is what business systems consume. Layout-aware Markdown keeps headings and tables so a model can reason over the document.
hints: For each requirement, name the consumer of the output: a vision step, a business API, or a language model reading the document. Each consumer wants a different shape.
Running OCR over pictures inside a PDF needs the pictures themselves in a usable form, not a text summary. An API that validates values needs a strict machine format.
The row about preserving headings and tables for reasoning needs a representation that keeps document structure while staying readable. One option is operational data and stays unused.
questions.deep: Produce both outputs from the same analysis when you can: JSON for deterministic automation and Markdown for retrieval and prompting. Treat quota metrics as monitoring data, which never substitutes for extracted content. Microsoft Learn: Content Understanding analyzer reference, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-understanding/concepts/analyzer-reference

questions.case:
Northwind Assist. Customer support agent modernization.

OVERVIEW
Northwind Traders sells consumer products in eleven European markets. Its current support chatbot answers only scripted questions, loses context when a customer changes topics, and frequently cites policies that have been superseded. Support managers want one agent experience for policy questions, order lookups, and refund requests.
The replacement will be built in Microsoft Foundry and hosted by an existing Azure App Service application. The application must serve customers and human support representatives through the same backend while preserving a separate conversation for each customer session.
The first production release is scheduled before the seasonal sales period. Northwind will initially keep human representatives responsible for unusual requests, but it expects the agent to handle routine policy retrieval and order-status work without manual intervention.

EXISTING ENVIRONMENT
The App Service has a system-assigned managed identity. A Foundry resource contains a project for the support team, and the project endpoint and model deployment name are supplied to the application through environment variables. Developers use DefaultAzureCredential locally and in Azure.
The project has a connection to an Azure AI Search service. Policy files are stored in Azure Blob Storage and ingested by an indexer. Each searchable chunk includes plain text, a vector, the parent document URL, market, product family, policy effective date, and policy expiration date.
The search service supports keyword, vector, and semantic ranking. Exact order-policy codes must remain searchable as literal values, while conceptual questions such as return eligibility should use hybrid retrieval. A nightly ingestion job adds newly approved documents and removes expired content from customer-facing results.
Order lookup and refund operations are exposed through HTTPS APIs described by an OpenAPI document. Each operation has a unique operationId. The refund API accepts an idempotency key so that retrying a timed-out tool call does not create a second refund.

REQUIREMENTS
Every policy answer must be grounded in current indexed evidence and include a link to the supporting policy. Retrieval must filter out documents that are not valid for the customer's market or that have expired. If evidence is absent or contradictory, the agent must say so and offer escalation.
A customer can ask a follow-up question without repeating the order number or market. Conversation state must therefore preserve the relevant context, but it must not leak information between customers or allow old tool results to silently override newer policy evidence.
User prompts and retrieved policy text must be checked for prompt attacks. Instructions embedded in uploaded or retrieved documents must be treated as untrusted data. A detected document attack should prevent that content from being sent to the model as grounding evidence.
Refunds of EUR 500 or less can proceed after the customer confirms the amount. Refunds above EUR 500 require a supervisor approval event before the refund API is invoked. A model recommendation alone never counts as approval, and a rejected request must not call the API.
All retrievals, model responses, tool arguments, tool results, approval decisions, and correlation identifiers must be traceable in Application Insights. Production code must not contain API keys, connection strings, or other long-lived secrets.

CONSTRAINTS
Traffic is usually modest but can increase rapidly during sales events. Northwind wants a pay-per-use model deployment for the initial release and will reassess provisioned capacity after it has several months of latency and token-usage measurements.
Model inference must remain within the EU data zone. Existing search and storage resources are in approved European regions. The operations team can implement retries for transient throttling, but it cannot move customer data to another geography to obtain extra capacity.
The support engineering team can assign narrowly scoped data-plane roles, but it wants to avoid custom credential rotation or unnecessary administrator intervention. Any access design must use the App Service identity and the smallest practical resource or project scope.
questions.prompt: Case study, Northwind Assist. Which two actions should you take to let the App Service call Foundry and query the search index without storing credentials? Choose two.
options: Assign the managed identity the minimum required Foundry and Search data-plane roles
Use the managed identity but assign only control-plane Reader on the Foundry and Search resources
Store both service keys in Key Vault and let the App Service retrieve them at startup
Use DefaultAzureCredential in the application
answer: Use DefaultAzureCredential in the application
Assign the managed identity the minimum required Foundry and Search data-plane roles
questions.explain: DefaultAzureCredential can use the App Service managed identity in Azure, and the minimum required Foundry and Search data-plane roles let that identity make calls. A control-plane Reader role does not allow data calls, and keys kept in Key Vault are still long-lived secrets.
questions.teach: Keyless access means the application proves who it is with a managed identity instead of a stored secret. The Azure Identity library's DefaultAzureCredential picks that identity up when the code runs in Azure. What the identity may then do is decided by role assignments, and data-plane roles are the ones that allow actually calling a service, as opposed to managing it.
hints: The requirement is that the app reaches two services without storing any credential. Split that into two jobs: how the code obtains a token, and what permission the token's owner has.

Moving a key into a vault only relocates the secret, and a role that lets someone see a resource in the portal does not allow data calls on it. Check each option for whether it really removes stored secrets and really grants permission to call.
Pick one option for the code side and one for the permission side, and make sure the permission side is data-plane and as narrow as possible.
questions.deep: Assign roles at the narrowest scope that works, for example the project or the individual index, and allow a few minutes for propagation. Locally, the same code runs with your developer sign-in because DefaultAzureCredential tries several sources in order. Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Foundry architecture, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/architecture

questions.prompt: Case study, Northwind Assist. Which retrieval approach best meets the policy-answer requirement?
options: Use hybrid retrieval with semantic reranking and pass document URLs and excerpts to the agent
Use hybrid retrieval with semantic reranking but pass only excerpt text, without source identifiers, to the agent
Use keyword-only retrieval with semantic reranking and return document URLs with each result
Use vector-only retrieval, return source URLs, and rely on embeddings for exact policy identifiers
answer: Use hybrid retrieval with semantic reranking and pass document URLs and excerpts to the agent
questions.explain: Hybrid retrieval covers exact terms and semantic similarity. Semantic reranking improves relevance, while returned URLs and excerpts give the model evidence it can cite.
questions.teach: Retrieval for grounded answers combines methods. Keyword search is precise for exact terms and identifiers, vector search finds conceptually similar text, and semantic ranking reorders the merged results for relevance. For the answer to be citable, the agent also needs the source identifiers and the excerpts, not just text.
hints: The case has two retrieval needs that pull in different directions: exact policy codes must still be found literally, and conceptual questions need meaning-based matching. Keep both in mind.
Options that rely on only one retrieval method give up one of those needs. Options that pass along text without source identifiers cannot support the requirement to link to the supporting policy.
The best answer combines the retrieval styles, reranks, and hands over both the source links and the excerpts.
questions.deep: Hybrid queries run keyword and vector searches in parallel and merge them with Reciprocal Rank Fusion before the semantic reranker. Apply the market and expiry filters in the query so ineligible documents never reach the model. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search vector search overview, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-overview

questions.prompt: Case study, Northwind Assist. How should the refund process be implemented?
options: Pause only when the model reports low confidence; otherwise let the agent execute the refund directly
Use a human-in-the-loop workflow that pauses before refund execution when the amount exceeds EUR 500
Require a second agent to approve the first agent's recommendation before the refund tool executes
Execute the refund with an idempotency key, then require a supervisor to approve the completed transaction
answer: Use a human-in-the-loop workflow that pauses before refund execution when the amount exceeds EUR 500
questions.explain: A human-in-the-loop step creates a real approval boundary before a consequential write operation. Notification after execution is only auditing, not authorization.
questions.teach: A human-in-the-loop step stops a workflow at a defined point until a person decides. For an action with side effects, such as a refund, the stop must come before the tool call runs. Approval after execution can record what happened but cannot prevent it.
hints: The requirement says refunds above a threshold need supervisor approval before the API is invoked. The important word is before. Check each option for when the human decision happens.
A design that notifies a supervisor after the money has moved is an audit trail, not an approval. Triggering a pause only on the model's own confidence does not depend on the amount at all.
A second agent is still an automated decision, not a supervisor. Look for the design that pauses for a person at the right point and for the stated condition.
questions.deep: Refunds also need an idempotency key so that a retry after a timeout cannot pay twice, as the case states. The approval record should capture who approved, when, and the exact amount and order, and a rejection must end the flow without calling the API. This was a preview feature when the source bank was checked, so confirm its current status on Microsoft Learn before relying on it. Microsoft Learn: Foundry workflows, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/workflow
