questions.explain: Function calling never runs your code: the model only proposes a call, your app executes it and sends back the result. When you want the service itself to make the call, you use an OpenAPI tool or an MCP tool. Foundry does not upload or sandbox your function, Code Interpreter is unrelated, and a JSON Schema describes parameters; it is not executable.
questions.teach: Agent tools split into two camps. In one camp the model decides a tool is needed and hands control back to your application, which does the real work in its own process and returns the output so the model can finish. In the other camp the service reaches out to a remote endpoint itself, using a description or protocol you registered and credentials stored in a project connection. Knowing which camp a tool belongs to tells you where the code runs and where failures appear.
hints: Think about what the service actually knows about a function tool. It only has a name, a description and a parameter schema. Ask yourself whether that is enough information to execute anything, or only enough to describe a call.

Now think about the opposite case. Some tools give the service a full address and contract for a remote endpoint, either a REST description file or an open tool protocol. With that, the service can make the request without your app.

Rule out the options that confuse unrelated features. A schema is a description of inputs, not a program, and the sandboxed Python tool is a separate feature that has nothing to do with whether a function tool works.
questions.deep: Because your app runs the function, your app also owns its security: validate the arguments the model produced, check the caller's permissions, and never pass model output straight into a shell or SQL statement. With OpenAPI and MCP tools that responsibility moves to the connection's auth and to require_approval settings.

questions.prompt: A colleague says that switching an Azure AI Search query from vector to hybrid has turned on semantic ranking. Which statement is accurate?
options: Hybrid search always includes semantic ranking, so no further change is needed
Hybrid merges keyword and vector results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion; semantic ranking is a separate re-ranking layer that needs a semantic configuration
Hybrid search replaces BM25 with a language model, which is what semantic ranking means
Semantic ranking only works on pure vector queries, so hybrid disables it
answer: Hybrid merges keyword and vector results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion; semantic ranking is a separate re-ranking layer that needs a semantic configuration
questions.explain: Hybrid runs a BM25 keyword query and a vector query and fuses the two ranked lists with RRF. The semantic ranker is an optional extra step that re-scores the top results with a language model and needs a semantic configuration. Hybrid does not include it, does not replace BM25, and does not disable it; the best RAG setup uses both together.
questions.teach: Azure AI Search offers four retrieval ideas. Full-text search uses BM25 keyword matching. Vector search compares embeddings for meaning. Hybrid runs both in one request and merges the two result lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). The semantic ranker is different in kind: it does not retrieve anything itself, it takes the top results from whatever query ran and re-orders them with a language model, adding captions and answers.
hints: Separate retrieving from re-ordering. Ask which of these features actually finds candidate documents, and which one only takes an existing list and shuffles it into a better order.

The word hybrid describes mixing two retrieval methods, one based on exact words and one based on embeddings. Think about how two ranked lists would be combined into one, and whether a language model is needed for that.
The re-ordering feature has its own setting on the index that names the title, content and keyword fields it should read. If hybrid switched it on automatically, that setting would not need to exist.
questions.deep: In a request, semantic ranking is opted into with queryType semantic plus a semanticConfiguration name, and it can sit on top of a hybrid query. It re-ranks only the top 50 results, so poor first-stage recall cannot be rescued by the ranker. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Search hybrid ranking, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/hybrid-search-ranking

questions.prompt: An extraction prompt returns slightly different field values on each run. The team has been lowering both temperature and top_p in alternate experiments and cannot tell which change helped. What should they do?
options: Keep lowering both values together until the output stops changing
Set temperature high and top_p low so the two settings cancel each other out
Tune temperature only, leave top_p at its default, and lower temperature for extraction
Raise the frequency penalty instead, because it controls randomness
answer: Tune temperature only, leave top_p at its default, and lower temperature for extraction
questions.explain: Temperature and top_p both control sampling randomness, so the guidance is to change one and leave the other alone. For extraction and factual tasks, a low temperature gives more stable output. Changing both at once makes results impossible to attribute, opposing settings do not cancel cleanly, and frequency penalty reduces repetition rather than randomness.
questions.teach: A model picks each next token by sampling from a probability distribution. Temperature reshapes that distribution: low values make the most likely token win almost every time, high values flatten it for more variety. Top_p, or nucleus sampling, limits sampling to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. Both knobs affect the same thing, which is why vendors recommend adjusting only one of them. Structured outputs with a JSON schema are the companion fix for reliable field shapes.
hints: Notice the experiment design problem first. When two settings that affect the same behaviour are changed in turns, any improvement could come from either one. Ask how a careful engineer would isolate the effect.
Both settings control how adventurous token sampling is. Because they overlap, the usual advice is to pick one of them as your control and leave the other at its default value.

For extraction you want the most predictable output possible, so the remaining knob should move towards its conservative end. The penalty settings discourage repeated words, which is a different problem.
questions.deep: Even at temperature 0, outputs can vary slightly because of non-deterministic GPU math and batching; a seed parameter improves but does not guarantee reproducibility. Reasoning models ignore or reject temperature and top_p and use reasoning_effort instead, so check the model before setting them.

questions.prompt: Which two problems are good reasons to fine-tune a model in Foundry rather than rely on prompts or RAG? Choose two.
options: Every answer must follow a strict house format and brand voice that prompts alone do not hold reliably
The assistant must know prices that change several times a day
A large model's quality must be kept while moving the workload to a smaller, cheaper model
Users try to jailbreak the assistant with role-play prompts
The assistant must answer from documents uploaded last week
answer: Every answer must follow a strict house format and brand voice that prompts alone do not hold reliably
A large model's quality must be kept while moving the workload to a smaller, cheaper model
questions.explain: Fine-tuning shapes style, format and behaviour, and it is the tool for distilling a large model into a cheaper one. Fast-changing prices and last week's documents are knowledge gaps that RAG fills, because fine-tuning does not add fresh knowledge well. Jailbreaks are handled by Prompt Shields, not by retraining.
questions.teach: Fine-tuning updates a model's weights from example data. It is good at teaching consistent habits: an output shape, a tone, a domain vocabulary, or how to behave on a narrow task. It is also used for distillation, where a big model's answers train a smaller model to reach similar quality at lower cost. It is weak at storing facts, especially facts that change, because every change would need another training run.
hints: Sort each option into one of three buckets: missing or changing knowledge, safety attacks, and behaviour or cost. Only one bucket is what retraining weights is good at.

Anything that changes daily or weekly would force you to retrain again and again, and the model might still blend old and new facts. Those problems belong to the technique that injects documents at query time.
Attacks hidden in user prompts are caught by a dedicated safety filter. What remains are a habit the model must follow every time and a plan to get similar quality from a smaller model.
questions.deep: Before fine-tuning, prove that prompts with few-shot examples and structured outputs are not enough, and keep a held-out evaluation set to compare the tuned model against the base. A fine-tuned deployment is billed per hour of hosting as well as per token in many regions, which changes the cost picture for low-traffic apps.

questions.prompt: Reviewers have collected thousands of prompts, each with one answer they preferred and one they rejected. You want the model to favour the preferred style. Which fine-tuning method fits this data?
options: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
Direct preference optimization (DPO)
Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT)
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
answer: Direct preference optimization (DPO)
questions.explain: DPO trains on pairs of preferred and rejected responses, which is exactly this data. SFT needs single ideal prompt and response examples, RFT targets reasoning models and learns from a grader's scores, and RAG is not fine-tuning at all; it adds retrieved documents at query time.
questions.teach: Foundry offers three fine-tuning methods. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns from examples of a prompt and the one correct response. Direct preference optimization (DPO) learns from comparisons: for a prompt, which of two responses humans liked better. Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) is for reasoning models and learns from a grader that scores attempts on hard tasks. The shape of the data you already have usually tells you which method to pick.
hints: Look closely at the shape of each training record. It is not a single right answer per prompt; it is two candidate answers with a judgement about which one was better.

One method learns by copying single ideal examples, another learns from a grader that scores attempts on reasoning tasks, and a third learns directly from comparisons between two answers. Match the record shape to the method.
One option is not a training method at all. It changes what goes into the prompt at query time rather than changing the model's weights, so it cannot learn a preference from comparison data.
questions.deep: A common recipe is SFT first to teach the task and format, then DPO on top to nudge style towards what reviewers prefer. DPO avoids training a separate reward model, which is why it is cheaper than classic reinforcement learning from human feedback.

questions.prompt: A contract says that prompts and completions for a claims assistant must be processed only in the Sweden Central region. A developer chose Global Standard because it has the highest default quota. Which deployment type meets the contract with pay-per-token billing?
options: Global Standard
Data Zone Standard
Standard (regional)
Global Batch
answer: Standard (regional)
questions.explain: Standard (regional) keeps processing inside the one region of the deployment and bills per token. Global Standard may process data in any Azure region, so it is never a residency answer. Data Zone Standard keeps data inside the EU or US data zone, which is wider than one region, and Global Batch is global and asynchronous.
questions.teach: A deployment type decides where inference runs and how you pay. Global types route each request to any Azure region with capacity, which gives the highest quota and lowest price but no location promise. Data Zone types keep processing inside a Microsoft data zone such as the EU or the US. Standard, also called regional, keeps processing inside the single region where you created the deployment. Data at rest stays in your resource's region in all cases; the type is about where processing happens.
hints: Find the strictest word in the requirement. The contract names one specific region, not a continent or a group of countries, and the answer must be at least that strict.

Rank the location promise of each family from widest to narrowest: anywhere in Azure, inside a data zone such as the EU, and inside a single region. Only the narrowest promise satisfies a single-region contract.
Quota and price are tempting, but they never override a residency rule. The asynchronous option is also global, so it fails for the same reason as the developer's original pick.
questions.deep: Regional Standard often has lower quota and later model availability than Global, so check that the model you need is offered in that region before promising the contract. Azure Policy can deny deployment SKUs such as GlobalStandard to stop this mistake from recurring.

questions.prompt: A user's request for violent instructions was blocked before the model produced any text. A developer insists content filters only inspect model output. Which statement is accurate?
options: Content filters check both the user prompt and the model completion, and Prompt Shields add detection for jailbreaks and indirect attacks
Content filters only check completions, so the block must have come from a custom blocklist
Content filters only check prompts, and completions are checked by groundedness detection
Prompt Shields replace content filters, so the harm categories no longer apply to prompts
answer: Content filters check both the user prompt and the model completion, and Prompt Shields add detection for jailbreaks and indirect attacks
questions.explain: Foundry content filters scan the input prompt and the output completion for hate, sexual, violence and self-harm at set severity levels, so a harmful prompt can be stopped before generation. Prompt Shields are an extra layer for jailbreaks and attacks hidden in documents. Blocklists and groundedness detection exist but did not cause this, and Prompt Shields do not replace the harm filters.
questions.teach: Responsible AI controls in Foundry run on both sides of the model. The harm filters classify text into four categories (hate, sexual, violence, self-harm) and four severity levels (safe, low, medium, high), and each can be configured separately for input and output. Add-ons cover specific threats: Prompt Shields for user jailbreaks and indirect document attacks, protected material detection, groundedness detection, custom blocklists and PII detection.
hints: Start from the evidence in the scenario. The block happened before any text was generated, so ask what could have been inspected at that moment. Only one side of the conversation existed.

Now recall the four harm categories and where they can be configured. Each category has separate threshold settings for the incoming text and for the generated text, which tells you both sides are checked.

Finally, separate the general harm filters from the specialised add-ons. One add-on targets attempts to override instructions, another checks whether answers match sources, and neither replaces the core filters.
questions.deep: When a prompt is filtered, the API returns HTTP 400 with a content_filter error code; when a completion is filtered, the response arrives with finish_reason content_filter. Handle both paths in client code so users see a helpful message instead of a crash. Microsoft Learn: Azure AI Content Safety overview, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/content-safety/overview

questions.prompt: Exam answers sometimes use older product names. Match each old name to the current Foundry concept it maps to.
rows: Azure OpenAI Service resource that hosts model deployments
Azure AI Studio, the browser portal for building apps
Cognitive Services such as Language, Speech and Translator
Hub-based project
options: Foundry resource
Foundry portal
Foundry Tools
Foundry project
Azure Machine Learning workspace
Azure API Management
answer: Foundry resource
Foundry portal
Foundry Tools
Foundry project
questions.explain: Model deployments now live on the Foundry resource, the old AI Studio portal is the Foundry portal, the prebuilt Cognitive Services are Foundry Tools, and the hub-based project is replaced by the Foundry project inside a Foundry resource. Azure Machine Learning and API Management are real services but are not what these names became.
questions.teach: Microsoft has renamed its AI platform several times. Today the top-level Azure resource is the Foundry resource (kind AIServices), which holds model deployments, networking and identity. Inside it, Foundry projects hold agents, connections, evaluations and files. Prebuilt services such as Language, Speech, Vision and Translator are Foundry Tools. On the exam, when an old-name option and a Foundry-native option both work, prefer the Foundry-native one.
hints: Begin with the row about where model deployments live. Today that job belongs to the top-level Azure resource that also carries keys, identity and networking settings, not to the workspace inside it.
The old studio was a website, so its new name is also a website. The prebuilt language, speech and translation services were renamed as a family of tools you call for standard tasks.
The last row is the old working boundary for agents and connections. Its successor is the working boundary inside the top-level resource. Two options are unrelated services and stay unused.
questions.deep: Hub-based projects still exist for some Azure Machine Learning style workloads, but new agent work uses Foundry projects, whose endpoint looks like https://<resource>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project>. Role names changed too, so scripts should assign roles by GUID. Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Foundry architecture, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/architecture

questions.prompt: You start a new Foundry agent project today. A sample you found uses threads.create, messages.create and runs.create_and_process. Which approach should the new project use for conversation state?
options: Copy the sample, because the thread, message and run model is the long-term API
Use conversations with the Responses API, because classic agents are deprecated and retire on March 31, 2027
Store the full history in the system message on every call instead of using any state API
Use threads for short chats and conversations only for long chats
answer: Use conversations with the Responses API, because classic agents are deprecated and retire on March 31, 2027
questions.explain: The new Foundry agent API keeps state in conversations and calls agents through the OpenAI-compatible Responses API. The classic thread, message and run API is deprecated and retires on March 31, 2027, so new work should not build on it. Stuffing the history into the system message wastes tokens, and there is no rule that splits threads and conversations by chat length.
questions.teach: Foundry agents have two vocabularies. The classic API created an agent, then a thread, added messages to it, and started a run to get a reply. The new API defines an agent as model plus instructions plus tools and keeps short-term memory in a conversation, called through the Responses API. Exam questions may still show classic code, so you should read both, but new designs use the newer one.
hints: Notice that the sample uses three separate objects to hold one chat and produce one reply. Ask whether that pattern is the current design or an older one that Microsoft has scheduled for retirement.
The newer agent API borrows its shape from the OpenAI-compatible interface, where one call produces a response and a separate object remembers the chat. Look for the option that names that pair.
Rule out the hand-rolled approach of pasting everything into the instructions, which grows token cost every turn. Also rule out any option that invents a split between two APIs based on chat length.
questions.deep: Long-term memory is a separate concern: the agent memory store (preview) or your own store such as Cosmos DB. With a Standard agent setup, conversations land in your own Cosmos DB account, which matters for residency and audit. Microsoft Learn: Foundry Agent Service runtime components, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/runtime-components

questions.prompt: An architect is planning a multi-agent system and asks you to confirm the facts. Which two statements are accurate? Choose two.
options: The A2A protocol lets agents on different platforms talk to each other, while MCP exposes tools to agents
Microsoft Agent Framework is the successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen
MCP is the protocol for delegating a task from one vendor's agent to another vendor's agent
A concurrent workflow runs specialist agents one after another, each consuming the previous output
Microsoft Agent Framework only builds prompt agents and cannot host code
answer: The A2A protocol lets agents on different platforms talk to each other, while MCP exposes tools to agents
Microsoft Agent Framework is the successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen
questions.explain: A2A is agent to agent across platforms and MCP is how agents reach tools, so swapping them is wrong. Agent Framework succeeds Semantic Kernel and AutoGen and is used for hosted, code-based agents. A concurrent workflow fans out to agents in parallel and fans the results back in; one-after-another is the sequential pattern.
questions.teach: Two open protocols appear on the exam. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an agent discover and call tools on a remote tool server. The Agent-to-Agent protocol (A2A) lets one agent hand work to another agent, even one built on a different platform. Microsoft Agent Framework is the code library for building agents and workflows; it merged ideas from Semantic Kernel and AutoGen. Its workflow patterns are sequential, concurrent (fan-out and fan-in), group chat and handoff, with human-in-the-loop checkpoints.
hints: Split the protocols by who is on the other end. One protocol connects an agent to a server full of callable tools, the other connects an agent to another agent that thinks for itself. Check that each option pairs them correctly.

Microsoft had two earlier open-source libraries for building agents, one focused on planning and plugins and one on multi-agent conversations. Its newer framework was announced as the next step for both.
Picture what the word concurrent means: several things happening at the same time, then their results gathered together. Running agents strictly in a chain is a different pattern with its own name.
questions.deep: Group chat lets several agents take turns in a shared conversation managed by a selector, while handoff transfers ownership of the task to one specialist at a time. Whatever the pattern, add max iterations, tool allow-lists and approval steps before irreversible actions. Microsoft Learn: Foundry workflows, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/workflow

questions.prompt: A bank's compliance team requires that agent conversations, uploaded files and vector stores live in Azure accounts the bank owns, reachable only over private networking. Which agent setup should you choose?
options: Basic agent setup with Microsoft-managed storage
Standard agent setup, bringing your own Cosmos DB, Storage account and Azure AI Search
Basic agent setup with a Global Standard model deployment
Standard agent setup that keeps Microsoft-managed storage but adds a private endpoint
answer: Standard agent setup, bringing your own Cosmos DB, Storage account and Azure AI Search
questions.explain: Standard agent setup stores conversations in your own Cosmos DB, files in your own Storage account and vectors in your own Azure AI Search, which you can lock behind private endpoints. Basic setup uses Microsoft-managed storage, so the bank would not own the data, and the deployment type does not change where agent state is stored. Standard setup is defined by bringing your own resources, so a version with Microsoft-managed storage is not a real option.
questions.teach: When you enable the Foundry Agent Service you choose how agent state is stored. Basic setup is quick: Microsoft manages the storage for conversations, files and vector stores. Standard setup connects the service to resources you own: Azure Cosmos DB for conversations (threads in the classic API), Azure Storage for files and Azure AI Search for vectors. Pick Standard when compliance, data residency, customer-managed keys or private networking are required.
hints: Read the requirement for ownership. The data must live in accounts the bank controls, so ask which setup lets you point the service at your own database, storage and search resources.
Think about each kind of agent state and which Azure service would hold it: chat history needs a database, uploaded documents need blob storage, and embeddings need a vector-capable search service.

The model's deployment type decides where inference runs, not where conversations are saved. And a setup cannot both bring your own resources and keep the managed ones, so check each option for that contradiction.
questions.deep: Standard setup with private networking also uses VNet injection so the agent runtime itself reaches your resources over private IPs, and the project's managed identity needs data-plane roles on Cosmos DB, Storage and Search. Choose the setup before you create agents, because moving existing agent state from Microsoft-managed storage to your own resources is not a simple switch.
